title: How things fly: wings push air down, and the air pushes them up

summary.text: A cheel can circle over a city for an hour, held up by air you cannot see. Everything that flies with wings stays up by pushing air down, and the air pushes back up on the wings. That upward push is called lift. Kites, paper planes, birds and flying seeds each use it in their own way. Scientists agree on what lift does, but still argue about the simplest way to explain it, and one famous explanation is wrong.
summary.art: A rooftop at sunset: a paper kite on a tight string, a black kite bird circling above the paper kite, a paper plane gliding past, and a winged mahogany seed spinning down, with faint arrows showing air being pushed downwards under each.

intro.hook: Hold a sheet of paper flat by two corners and drop it. Now crumple an identical sheet into a ball and drop it. Now fold a third sheet into a paper plane and throw it gently. Same paper. Why do they come down so differently?
intro.text: Look up on any sunny afternoon in an Indian city. You will probably see big brown birds circling high above, hardly flapping at all. They are black kites, called cheel in Hindi. They can stay up for an hour. A crow beside them flaps and flaps. A paper kite on a string climbs only when the wind blows. A seed from a mahogany tree spins down like a tiny helicopter. A cheel weighs about as much as a 1-kilogram packet of sugar. So how can it stay up in air that you cannot even see?
intro.art: A city sky with a cheel circling without flapping, a crow flapping hard, a patang on a string and a spinning winged seed, each with a question mark beside them.

outcomes: I can say that air is a real material that pushes, and that everything that flies pushes on the air.
I can name the four forces on a flying thing: lift, weight, drag and thrust. I can draw them as arrows.
I can explain that a wing or a kite stays up by pushing air downwards, so the air pushes it upwards.
I can run a fair test on a paper plane or a paper spinner, measure it, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can say how kites, paper planes, birds and flying seeds each stay up, and how they are different.
I can say what scientists agree about lift, which famous explanation is wrong, and what is still argued about.
I can follow flight out to air molecules, a helicopter on Mars, the first birds, and the people who made flying possible.

terms.meaning: The invisible gas all around us. It is made of countless tiny particles, called molecules, that move very fast and bump into everything.
terms.example: You feel air when a fan blows on you, or when you wave a notebook near your face.
terms.art: A child waving a notebook, with little dots of air bouncing off it.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. Forces make things start moving, stop, speed up, slow down or turn.
terms.example: Wind pushes a kite. Gravity pulls a falling seed down.
terms.art: A kite with a wind arrow pushing it and a string arrow pulling it.

terms.meaning: Moving through the air without touching the ground, for longer than a jump.
terms.example: A sparrow flying to the nest. A paper plane crossing the room.
terms.art: A sparrow mid-flight between a tree and a balcony.

terms.meaning: A wide, thin part that pushes air downwards as it moves through the air. Birds, bats, insects, planes and some seeds have wings.
terms.example: A bird's wing, a paper plane's wing and the papery wing on a drumstick seed.
terms.art: Three wings side by side: a bird's, a paper plane's and a seed's.

terms.meaning: The upward push of the air on a wing or a kite. It comes from the wing pushing air downwards.
terms.example: Lift holds up a flying pigeon, a glider and a jumbo jet.
terms.art: A wing with an arrow pointing up, labelled lift, and air arrows going down behind it.

terms.meaning: The pull of gravity on a thing, down towards the Earth. Every flying thing has weight.
terms.example: A paper clip on a paper plane adds a little weight to its nose.
terms.art: A paper plane with a downward arrow from its middle, labelled weight.

terms.meaning: The air pushing back against something moving through it. It slows things down. Drag is another name for air resistance.
terms.example: Running with an open umbrella, you feel the air drag it back.
terms.art: A child running with an umbrella, an arrow pointing backwards.

terms.meaning: A forward push that keeps a flying thing moving. It can come from flapping wings, a propeller or a jet engine.
terms.example: Your arm gives a paper plane its thrust when you throw it.
terms.art: A hand launching a paper plane, a forward arrow from the hand.

terms.meaning: To fly without flapping or an engine, slowly sinking through the air while moving forward.
terms.example: A paper plane glides. So does a flying lizard jumping between trees.
terms.art: A paper plane on a long gentle sloping path.

terms.meaning: To stay up, or even climb, without flapping, by riding on rising air.
terms.example: Cheels and vultures soar in circles high over cities on hot afternoons.
terms.art: A vulture circling inside a faint spiral of rising warm air.

terms.meaning: A bubble or column of warm air rising from hot ground. Soaring birds circle inside it to climb.
terms.example: Over a hot road or a dry field at midday, thermals rise and black kites circle in them.
terms.art: Wavy columns of warm air rising from a hot road, with birds circling at the top.

terms.meaning: How much the front edge of a wing or kite is raised into the oncoming air. A little tilt gives more lift. Too much tilt and the wing stops lifting well.
terms.example: Tilt your flat hand slightly in front of a fan and feel it pushed up.
terms.art: A hand held in front of a fan, front edge raised a little, an up arrow above it.

terms.meaning: When a wing is tilted too steeply, the air can't follow its top surface. The wing loses most of its lift and drops.
terms.example: A paper plane that swoops up steeply, stops and then falls has stalled.
terms.art: A paper plane pointing steeply up with swirly air tumbling off its top.

terms.meaning: The point where a thing balances. Its weight acts as if it were all there. For a plane to fly steadily, this point must be a little in front of the middle of its wings.
terms.example: Balance a paper plane on your fingertip. Where it balances is its balance point.
terms.art: A paper plane balanced on one fingertip, a dot marking the point.

terms.meaning: A light frame covered with paper or cloth that flies on the wind, held by a string. In India a paper kite is called a patang or guddi.
terms.example: On Makar Sankranti the skies over Ahmedabad and Hyderabad fill with kites.
terms.art: A diamond patang with a tail, its string running down to a child on a rooftop.

terms.meaning: How hard the air pushes on a surface. It comes from countless air molecules bumping into the surface.
terms.example: Air pressure keeps a balloon blown up from the inside.
terms.art: A balloon with tiny dots bouncing off the inside of its skin.

terms.meaning: A tiny group of atoms joined together. Air is mostly molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, far too small to see.
terms.example: Each breath you take holds more air molecules than there are grains of sand on all the world's beaches.
terms.art: A zoom from a breath of air to tiny pairs of balls zooming about.

terms.meaning: The light, strong covering of a bird. Wing feathers are stiff and shaped to push air. Fluffy feathers keep birds warm.
terms.example: A pigeon feather you find on a balcony.
terms.art: A long wing feather and a fluffy down feather side by side.

terms.meaning: Many flying birds have bones with air spaces inside, held up by thin struts. They are light but strong.
terms.example: A chicken leg bone from dinner is filled with soft marrow. A pigeon's wing bone is mostly air inside, crossed by thin struts.
terms.art: A cut-open bird bone showing struts like a bridge inside.

terms.meaning: Seeds with a thin, papery wing. When they fall, they spin or glide, so the wind can carry them further.
terms.example: Mahogany seeds spin down like helicopters. Drumstick seeds have three papery wings.
terms.art: A big-leaf mahogany seed spinning down, with a circular blur around the seed.

terms.meaning: A tuft of fine hairs on some seeds. It catches the air, so the seed falls very slowly and drifts on the wind.
terms.example: Dandelion seeds, and the silky fluff from an aak plant or a semal tree.
terms.art: A dandelion seed and an aak seed with their silky tufts, drifting.

terms.meaning: To stay in one place in the air. It takes a lot of work, because the wings must keep pushing air down all the time.
terms.example: A sunbird or a hoverfly hanging in front of a flower.
terms.art: A purple sunbird hovering by a hibiscus flower, wings blurred.

explanations.concept: Air is a real material that pushes
explanations.definition: Air is a real material, made of countless tiny moving particles called molecules. It takes up space, it has weight, and it pushes on everything it touches.
explanations.description: We can't see air, so it is easy to think of it as nothing. But push a glass upside down into a bucket of water. A tissue stuck inside stays dry, because the air in the glass keeps the water out. Run with a big piece of cardboard held flat in front of you. You feel the air pushing back. Air even has weight. The air in a small bedroom weighs about 35 kilograms, about as much as a child of ten. Flying is only possible because air is a real material. A wing has something to push on.
examples: A tissue stuck inside an upside-down glass stays dry under water.
A ceiling fan pushes air down, and you feel the breeze.
A blown-up balloon stays round because air inside pushes on its skin.
explanations.art: Three panels: a glass pushed upside down into a bucket with a dry tissue inside, a child running with cardboard held flat; a balloon with dots of air bouncing inside.
explanations.context: This card explains the first idea of the whole unit. Air is a real material that a wing can push on.

explanations.concept: Four forces on every flying thing
explanations.definition: A flying thing has four forces on it. Weight pulls it down. Lift pushes it up. Drag pushes it back. Thrust pushes it forward.
explanations.description: A force is a push or a pull. We draw each force as an arrow pointing the way it pushes. Weight is gravity pulling the flying thing towards the Earth. Lift is the air pushing it up. Drag is the air pushing back as it moves. Thrust is whatever pushes it forward. That can be a flapping wing, a propeller or your throwing arm. A glider has no thrust of its own. It keeps moving forward by slowly losing height, like a cycle rolling down a gentle slope. An English inventor, George Cayley, first drew these forces on a flying machine, around 1799.
examples: A pigeon flapping: their wings give both lift and thrust.
A paper plane after it leaves your hand: no more thrust, so it glides slowly down.
A kite: the wind gives the push, and the string holds it against the wind.
explanations.art: A paper plane with four arrows: lift up, weight down, thrust forward, drag back, each a different colour.
explanations.context: Every flying thing, from a sparrow to a jet, has the same four forces on them. This card names them and shows them as arrows.

explanations.concept: How a wing makes lift: it pushes air down
explanations.definition: A wing makes lift by turning the air that flows past it downwards. When the wing pushes air down, the air pushes the wing up. That push shows up as lower air pressure above the wing and higher air pressure below it.
explanations.description: Every push has an equal push back. Isaac Newton wrote this down in 1687, and it is called Newton's third law. When you swim, you push water backwards, and the water pushes you forwards. A wing works the same way with air. As it moves through the air, tilted slightly upwards at the front, it bends the air behind it downwards. The air pushes back, upwards, on the wing. That upward push is lift. How does the air push on the wing? Through air pressure. As the wing bends the air, the air presses a little less on the top of the wing and a little more on the bottom. Pushing air down and the difference in pressure are two ways of describing the same lift. Even a flat wing, like a paper plane's, can do this, as long as it is tilted a little. A helicopter shows it plainly. Stand near one and you feel a gale blowing down.
examples: Under a hovering helicopter, a strong wind blows straight down.
A flat paper plane wing still makes lift, because it is tilted a little.
A crow's downstroke pushes air down and back. The air pushes the crow up and forward.
explanations.art: A wing seen from the side, tilted slightly, smooth airflow lines curving down behind it, and a big up arrow on the wing.
explanations.context: This is the most important card in the unit. It explains, simply and correctly, how anything with wings stays up.

explanations.concept: Why the air speeds up over a wing: a famous puzzle
explanations.description: Scientists measure lift very well. Engineers use their sums to build planes that carry hundreds of people safely. So nobody doubts what wings do. The argument is about the best simple way to explain it. One explanation, found in many old books, is simply wrong. Here are the main ideas.
examples: Smoke filmed in a wind tunnel shows air over the top of a wing reaching the back first, long before the air underneath.
Paper planes have flat wings and fly well. Stunt planes can even fly upside down.

perspectives.who: The 'equal time' story, in many old books and websites
perspectives.explanation: The top of a wing is curved, so air going over it has further to travel. The two streams must meet again at the back at the same time. So the air on top must go faster. This is wrong. Nothing makes the two streams meet again. In real tests, air over the top races ahead and arrives at the back much sooner.

perspectives.who: Daniel Bernoulli, a Swiss scientist, in 1738
perspectives.explanation: Where air moves faster, it pushes less hard on the surfaces beside it. Over a wing, the air really does move faster, so it pushes less hard on top. The air underneath pushes harder. So the wing is pushed up. This is true. But on its own, it doesn't say why the air speeds up.
The wing turns air downwards, so the air pushes the wing upwards. This is also true. But on its own, it doesn't explain how a wing turns the air flowing over its top.

perspectives.who: Scientists today, such as Holger Babinsky at Cambridge in 2003 and Doug McLean at Boeing in 2012
perspectives.explanation: Bernoulli's idea and Newton's idea are two views of one thing. A wing bends the air. To bend moving air, there must be a difference in air pressure: lower above the wing, higher below. That same difference speeds up the air over the top. Some scientists still say no simple explanation is accepted by everyone. In 2020, an article in the magazine Scientific American said that nobody can yet explain lift in a way all experts agree on.

explanations.art: A wing in a wind tunnel with pulses of white smoke, where the pulse on top has raced ahead of the pulse underneath, with a red cross over the words 'equal time'.
explanations.context: Most people have heard an explanation of why wings work. This card is about which explanations are right, which one is wrong, and what is still argued about.

explanations.definition: A kite flies because the wind pushes on it while the string holds it back. The kite is tilted, so the wind is turned downwards and the kite is pushed upwards.
explanations.description: A kite has no engine and does not flap. Instead, the wind moves past it. The string pulls the kite back, so it can't simply be blown away. The tilted kite turns the wind downwards, and the wind pushes the kite up. If the string goes slack, the kite tumbles. If the wind stops, you can run, so the air still moves past the kite. A tail adds a little drag at the back. It keeps the kite's nose pointing into the wind, so it doesn't spin. Old stories from China say people made kites there more than 2,000 years ago. In India, kites fill the sky on Makar Sankranti in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Hyderabad, and on Independence Day in Delhi.
examples: A patang climbs when the string is pulled tight and drops when it goes slack.
On a still day you must run to fly a kite.
A kite that spins round and round often needs a longer tail.
explanations.art: A diamond kite with three arrows: wind pushing back, string pulling down and forward, and lift pushing up, and a tail streaming behind.
explanations.context: Kites fly with no engine and no flapping. This card explains the trick: the wind pushes, the string holds, and the tilt turns the push upwards.

explanations.concept: How paper planes and gliders fly
explanations.definition: A glider has no engine. It moves forward by slowly sliding down through the air, while its wings make lift. To fly steadily, its balance point must be a little in front of the middle of its wings.
explanations.description: Your arm gives a paper plane its thrust, but only for a moment. After that, it glides. It sinks a little all the time, and that sinking keeps it moving forward. A good glider sinks very slowly and travels far. Where the plane balances matters a lot. If the nose is too light, the plane swoops up, stalls and drops. If the nose is too heavy, it dives. A paper clip on the nose moves the balance point forward. Bending up the back edges of the wings a little lifts the nose. Real gliders work in the same way. They can stay up for hours by finding rising air, just like soaring birds.
examples: A paper plane that swoops up and drops needs a paper clip on its nose.
A paper plane that dives needs the back edges of its wings bent up a little.
Otto Lilienthal, a German engineer, made about 2,000 glider flights in the 1890s.
explanations.art: Three paper plane paths: one swooping up and dropping, one diving, one gliding long and smooth, each with its fix drawn beside it.
explanations.context: Paper planes are the easiest way to test flight at home. This card explains why some glide far and others swoop or dive.

explanations.concept: How birds fly: flapping, gliding and soaring
explanations.definition: Birds flap their wings to push air down and back, which gives them lift and thrust. Many birds also glide, and some soar on rising warm air without flapping at all.
explanations.description: On each downstroke, a bird sweeps their wings down and forward. The air is pushed down and back, so the bird is pushed up and forward. On the upstroke, the feathers twist and open to let air through. A bird's body is built for this. It has hollow bones with thin struts inside, and a big breastbone holding strong flying muscles. Its feathers are light but strong. Soaring birds like the black kite and the vulture hardly flap. On hot days, warm air rises from the ground in bubbles called thermals. The birds circle inside them and are carried up with the rising air. Then they glide down to the next thermal.
examples: Cheels circle high over Indian cities at midday, rising on thermals.
A sunbird hovers by a flower, flapping very fast.
Common swifts can stay in the air for about 10 months without landing. A Swedish study tracked them in 2016.
explanations.art: A crow's downstroke and upstroke in two frames, and beside it a black kite circling in a spiral of rising warm air above a hot city road.
explanations.context: Birds were flying for millions of years before people. This card explains how they flap, glide and soar.

chart.title: How wide some Indian birds' wings are, tip to tip (about)
chart.note: Rough sizes for a grown bird. Each bird is a little different.

explanations.definition: Many plants make seeds that fly, so the wind carries them far from the parent plant. Some float on parachutes of fine hairs. Some spin on one wing. Some glide on two wings.
explanations.description: A seed that lands under their parent has to share light and water with them. A seed that travels can find new ground. So plants have found many ways to fly. A dandelion seed hangs under a tuft of about a hundred fine bristles. In 2018, scientists in Edinburgh found that air flowing through the bristles makes a ring of swirling air above the seed. The ring holds the seed up, so they fall very slowly. A mahogany seed has one wing and spins while falling. In 2009, scientists filmed spinning maple seeds and found something new. The spinning makes a little whirl of air over the wing, which gives extra lift. Some seeds glide. The Javan cucumber, a climbing plant in Asia, makes a paper-thin seed with wings about 13 centimetres across, wider than your palm. They glide like a tiny plane. In the early 1900s, an Austrian inventor, Igo Etrich, built gliders shaped like it.
examples: Silky aak and semal fluff floats away on the wind.
Big-leaf mahogany seeds spin down like helicopters in many Indian cities.
Drumstick seeds have three papery wings.
explanations.art: Three seeds falling side by side: a dandelion seed under a faint swirling air ring, a mahogany seed spinning, and a wide Javan cucumber seed gliding.
explanations.context: Birds and planes are not the only flyers. This card is about seeds that float, spin and glide, and the surprising swirls of air they make.

explanations.definition: Some animals glide but can't flap. They spread out flaps of skin, or flatten their bodies, to glide from tree to tree.
explanations.description: Gliding saves time and energy. It is also safer than climbing down to the ground, where predators, the animals that hunt them, wait. India's forests have many gliders. The flying lizard of the Western Ghats spreads skin flaps held out on their ribs. The Indian giant flying squirrel stretches skin between their arms and legs. They can glide across gaps longer than a cricket pitch. The ornate flying snake jumps from a branch and flattens their body into a wide ribbon. They wiggle through the air in an S shape. Flying fish in the Indian Ocean leap out of the water and glide on large fins. None of them can stay up for long, because they make lift without any thrust.
examples: A flying lizard spreading their bright skin flaps.
A flying squirrel gliding at night between tall trees.
A flying snake flattening their body into a ribbon.
explanations.art: A forest scene at dusk: a flying squirrel gliding, a flying lizard with orange flaps, and a flying snake in an S shape between two trees.
explanations.context: Some animals fly without wings that flap. This card is about the gliding lizards, squirrels, snakes and fish of India.

explanations.concept: How did birds start to fly?
explanations.description: Birds came from small feathered dinosaurs, more than 150 million years ago. Most scientists agree on that, because of fossils like Archaeopteryx, found in Germany in 1861. But how did flapping flight begin? Half a wing can't lift a body. So what good was half a wing? Scientists have argued about this for more than a hundred years.
examples: Archaeopteryx had feathered wings, but also teeth, claws and a long bony tail.
Young chukar partridges flap their small wings to help them run up steep slopes.

perspectives.explanation: Small feathered dinosaurs climbed trees and glided down, like flying squirrels today. Over a very long time, gliding turned into flapping.
Small feathered dinosaurs ran fast on the ground. Flapping feathered arms helped them leap, balance and catch insects. Later, the flapping lifted them right off the ground.

perspectives.who: Kenneth Dial, an American scientist, in 2003
perspectives.explanation: Young partridges flap to run up tree trunks and steep rocks before they can fly. So even half a wing is useful. This may show how flight began. Other scientists are not sure, and the question is still open.

explanations.art: A small feathered dinosaur in two scenes: gliding down from a tree, and running fast up a slope while flapping their feathered arms.
explanations.context: Birds came from dinosaurs. This card asks how they first took to the air, a question scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: Deep down: lift is air molecules bumping
explanations.definition: Air pressure is the push of countless air molecules bumping into a surface. A wing gets lift because the molecules underneath bump into it harder than the molecules on top.
explanations.description: Zoom into the air and keep zooming. You reach molecules, tiny groups of atoms. In air, they are mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Each one zooms about at roughly 500 metres every second. That is faster than a passenger jet. Every bit of your skin is being bumped by them all the time, from every side. We call that steady push air pressure. Usually the bumps are the same on all sides, so we don't notice them. A moving wing changes the pattern. Underneath, the bumps push a little harder. On top, they push a little less. The difference is lift. So a jumbo jet is held up by countless tiny bumps.
examples: A balloon stays round because molecules inside bump on its skin.
High on a mountain, there are fewer molecules, so wings and lungs both have to work harder.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps, from a plane to its wing, to a close-up of the wing's skin, to tiny molecules bouncing off it, more crowded underneath than on top.
explanations.context: This card zooms in far past anything we can see, to find out what lift really is deep down.

explanations.definition: Wings need air to push on. Where there is no air, as in space, wings do nothing. Where there is thin air, as on Mars, wings must move very fast.
explanations.description: In space there is no air at all, so a plane's wings would have nothing to push. Rockets work differently. They throw hot gas out backwards very fast, and the gas pushes the rocket forwards. Mars has air, but only about one hundredth as much as Earth. In 2021, NASA flew a small helicopter called Ingenuity on Mars. It was the first powered flight on another planet. Its blades spun about 2,400 times a minute, many times faster than a ceiling fan. The team was led by MiMi Aung, an engineer who grew up partly in Myanmar. Its chief engineer, Bob Balaram, studied at IIT Madras. Ingenuity was meant to fly 5 times. It flew 72 times. Saturn's moon Titan has thick air and weak gravity. NASA plans to send a flying drone there, called Dragonfly.
examples: Ingenuity's first flight, on 19 April 2021, lasted about 40 seconds.
Astronauts on the Moon can't fly a kite, because the Moon has no air.
explanations.art: A small helicopter with long blades hovering above red Martian rocks, a rover watching from nearby, a pale Sun in a dusty pink sky.
explanations.context: Everything in this unit flies by pushing on air. This card asks what happens on worlds with thin air, or none at all.

chart.title: How much air fills the same box, on Earth and on Mars
chart.note: Mars has only about 1 hundredth as much air as Earth. So wings there must spin very fast to push enough air down.

explanations.concept: How insects fly, and the bumblebee puzzle
explanations.definition: Insects fly by flapping their wings very fast and twisting them. Each stroke makes a small whirl of air over the wing, which gives much more lift than a still wing could.
explanations.description: A housefly beats their wings about 200 times every second. That makes the buzz you hear. Small wings flapping so fast work differently from big airplane wings. As each wing sweeps, a little whirlwind forms along its front edge and clings to it. That whirl gives extra lift. For a long time, nobody understood this. People joked that science said bumblebees should not be able to fly. In 1999, Michael Dickinson and his team in California built a giant robot fly wing, flapping in a tank of oil. They measured the forces and showed how insect wings make so much lift.
examples: A mosquito's whine is the sound of their wings beating hundreds of times a second.
Dragonflies can fly backwards, and each of their four wings can move on its own.
explanations.art: A bumblebee with blurred wings, and a close-up of one wing with a small swirl of air clinging to its front edge.
explanations.context: Insects were the first animals to fly, more than 300 million years ago. This card explains their trick, and an old joke about bumblebees.

agreed.text: Air is a real material. It takes up space, has weight and pushes on things.
agreed.evidence: A tissue stays dry in an upside-down glass pushed under water. A blown-up ball weighs a little more than a flat one, on a very fine scale.

agreed.text: Everything that flies with wings stays up by pushing air downwards.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measure the air flowing down behind wings, in wind tunnels and around real planes. Under a hovering helicopter, you can feel it.

agreed.text: The 'equal time' explanation of lift is wrong.
agreed.evidence: Wind tunnel films with pulses of smoke show air over the top of a wing reaching the back much sooner than the air underneath. Holger Babinsky at Cambridge made one in 2012.

agreed.text: People first flew in a powered plane that they could steer in 1903.
agreed.evidence: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew four times on 17 December 1903, at Kitty Hawk in the USA. Photographs and witnesses recorded it. The first flight lasted 12 seconds.

chart.title: The Wright brothers' four flights on 17 December 1903
chart.note: Flights 1 and 3 were flown by Orville. Flights 2 and 4 were flown by Wilbur.

agreed.evidence: Fossils show small dinosaurs with feathers, wishbones and hollow bones, just like birds. Archaeopteryx, found in 1861, has a mix of bird and dinosaur features.

challenging.claim: Air over the top of a wing goes faster because it must meet the air from underneath at the back at the same time.
challenging.who: Many older textbooks, websites and even some pilot training books
challenging.for: Air over the top of a wing really does go faster. And the curved top looks like a longer path.
challenging.against: Nothing makes the two streams of air meet again. Films of smoke show the air on top arriving much sooner. The sums don't work either. The 'equal time' speed is far too small to hold a plane up.
challenging.context: This card is about the most famous explanation of how wings work, and why scientists say it is wrong.

challenging.claim: Wings only lift because their tops are curved.
challenging.who: A common idea, from pictures of wing shapes
challenging.for: Most bird and plane wings are curved on top, and curved wings do lift well.
challenging.against: Paper planes have flat wings and still fly. Stunt planes fly upside down, with the curved side underneath. What matters most is that the wing turns the air downwards. Tilt matters as much as shape.
challenging.context: Most wings are curved on top. This card asks whether the curve is the whole secret.

challenging.claim: Science says a bumblebee should not be able to fly.
challenging.who: A popular saying, from a quick sum repeated in a French book in 1934
challenging.for: If you treat a bee's wing like a still airplane wing, the sum says it is too small to hold the bee up.
challenging.against: Bee wings are not still. They flap and twist very fast, making whirls of air that give extra lift. In 1999, Michael Dickinson's robot fly wing measured this. Science never said bees can't fly. One rough sum did.
challenging.context: You may have heard that science can't explain how bumblebees fly. This card is about where that saying came from.

challenging.claim: The Wright brothers were the first people to fly.
challenging.who: Most history books, and the USA
challenging.for: In 1903 the Wrights made powered, controlled flights, with photographs and witnesses. They also worked out how to steer a plane in the air.
challenging.against: People had flown long before in balloons, from 1783, and in gliders. In 1906, Alberto Santos-Dumont flew a plane in Paris in front of a big crowd. Many people in Brazil call him the first. Some say Gustave Whitehead flew in 1901, but there is little good evidence for that.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for the first flight. The answer depends on what you count as flying.

challenging.claim: Shivkar Bapuji Talpade flew an unmanned plane over Mumbai's Chowpatty beach in 1895.
challenging.who: Later books, newspaper stories and a 2015 Hindi film
challenging.for: Talpade was a real Sanskrit scholar and teacher in Mumbai, who was interested in flight.
challenging.against: No newspaper from 1895 reported such a flight. No photographs, drawings or witnesses' records have been found. Historians say the story first appeared many years later.
challenging.context: This card is about a story that an Indian teacher flew a plane eight years before the Wright brothers.

challenging.claim: An old Sanskrit book, the Vaimanika Shastra, describes real flying machines from ancient India.
challenging.for: Old Indian stories, like the Pushpaka Vimana in the Ramayana, describe flying chariots. People have always dreamed of flying.
challenging.against: The book was written down in the early 1900s, not in ancient times. In 1974, engineers at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru studied its designs. They found that none of them could fly. The flying chariots in old stories are wonderful stories, not records.
challenging.context: This card is about a book said to describe ancient Indian aircraft, and what engineers found when they checked it.

challenging.claim: Things heavier than air can never fly. Only balloons can.
challenging.who: Many people, and some well-known scientists, in the 1890s
challenging.for: At that time, every attempt at a heavier-than-air flying machine with an engine had failed. Some inventors died trying.
challenging.against: Birds are heavier than air, and they fly. In 1903 the Wrights flew. Today a big plane weighing as much as 80 elephants can fly. Wings, not lightness, hold it up.
challenging.context: Before 1903, many people thought heavy machines could never fly. This card is about why they changed their minds.

big_questions.q: If air is invisible, how do we know it is really there?
big_questions.hint: Push an upside-down glass into water, with a tissue stuck inside. What keeps the tissue dry?

big_questions.q: Could you fly a kite on the Moon?
big_questions.hint: What does a kite push on? Is there any of it on the Moon?

big_questions.q: Why can a heavy jumbo jet fly, but a light ball of paper just falls?
big_questions.hint: Is it about how heavy it is, or about whether it pushes air down?

big_questions.q: Plants can't walk, yet their seeds travel across rivers and fields. What else in nature travels without legs?
big_questions.hint: Think of clouds, pollen, spider babies on silk threads and the smell of food.

big_questions.q: People dreamed of flying for thousands of years before they could. Why do you think humans wanted to fly so much?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Pushpaka Vimana, Icarus, and how the world looks from a rooftop.

big_questions.q: A bird flies inside a closed box that sits on a weighing scale. Does the box weigh less while the bird is flying?
big_questions.hint: The bird's wings push air down. Where does that air push next?

big_questions.q: Glass-coated kite string cuts thousands of birds every festival. Who should share the sky, and how?
big_questions.hint: Whose sky is it: the people's, the birds', or everyone's?

big_questions.q: Ostriches, penguins and the dodo lost the power to fly. Why might a bird stop needing to fly?
big_questions.hint: Flying uses lots of energy. What if there were no hunters to escape, or food was on the ground?

big_questions.q: The 'equal time' explanation of wings was in books for decades, and it was wrong. How can we tell when an explanation is right?
big_questions.hint: What would you need to see? Remember the smoke films in a wind tunnel.
Crows have been seen sliding down snowy roofs again and again, as if for fun. How could we ever know what a bird feels?

big_questions.q: Who should get the credit for a great invention: the first to try, the first to succeed, or the first to tell the world?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Wright brothers, of Santos-Dumont, and of Charlie Taylor, the mechanic who built the Wrights' engine in six weeks.

story.title: The Kite Who Watched the Kites
story.note: Delhi really does fill with paper kites every Independence Day, and black kites really do soar over the old city. Glass-coated kite string really injures many birds, and the Charity Birds Hospital in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, really treats them. The narrator, Farah, Bilal and everything that happens to them are made up.
text: I am a kite. Not the paper kind. I am the older kind, the kind with feathers. People in Delhi call me cheel. The English named their paper toys after my family, long ago, because the toys hang in the wind the way we do.

I live on the broken water tank above a sweet shop in the old city. From there I can see the whole jumble of rooftops, the domes of the mosque, and the river far away. On most days the sky belongs to my family and to the pigeons. But every year, on the fifteenth of August, the people climb onto their roofs, and the sky fills up with paper.

That year I watched a girl called Farah. She was nine, and she had one kite. It was pink, with a torn corner patched with tape. Her cousin Bilal had six kites and a big wooden spool of string that glittered in the sun. I knew that glitter. It was glass, ground fine and glued onto the thread, so that his string could cut other people's strings. It can cut feathers too.

Farah's kite would not fly. She held it above her head and ran across the roof, and it bumped along behind her like a tired dog. She threw it up into the air, and it turned over and fell between two water pots. Bilal laughed. 'Your kite is scared of the sky,' he said.
I did not laugh. I had been young once, and I had fallen too.

The sun was high. Over the hot roofs and the hot roads, warm air was beginning to rise in great invisible bubbles. I could feel one under the tank, like a breath. I stepped off, spread my wings, and did not flap. I tilted the front edges of my wings up, just a little, and leaned on the rising air. It pushed up under me. I turned in a slow circle, and the bubble carried me up, round and round, until Farah's roof was the size of a chapati.

From up there, I saw her stop running. She was looking at me. She shaded her eyes with one hand and watched me hang in the sky without moving a feather. I twisted my forked tail a little, to keep my head pointing into the breeze. I could feel her wondering.

Then she did something clever. All morning she had run along with the wind, so the kite only drifted lazily after her. Now she stood still, with the wind blowing on her back. She called her little brother and put the kite in his hands. 'Carry it to the far edge,' she said. 'Hold it up high, with its face to the wind. Let go only when I say.' He walked away across the roof, and she let out string as he went, until it stretched between them, tight. The pink paper faced the breeze, the way I always face it.
'Now!'

He let go. She did not run. She pulled. The wind pushed the pink kite back, and the string held it, and the kite had nowhere to go but up. It shot up past the washing line, past the neighbour's satellite dish, wobbling and then steadying. Farah let out a little string, then pulled again, and it climbed again. Whenever the string went slack, the kite began to sag. Whenever she drew it tight, it rose. She was laughing out loud.

So that was the secret she found. A kite does not fly in spite of the string. It flies because of it. The wind pushes, the string holds, and the tilted paper turns the push into an upward push. Mine is the same trick, without the string. I lean on the moving air, and the air holds me.

For an hour the sky was perfect. Hundreds of paper kites hung over the old city, red and yellow and green, and my family wheeled among them. Then the fighting began. The kite fighters crossed their strings and sawed, and kites came loose and drifted away over the rooftops. People cheered. Bilal cut three kites down, one after another.

I did not see the fourth string. It was loose, trailing from a kite that had already been cut. It drifted across the sky like a spider's thread, and the glass in the thread caught the light a moment too late. It wrapped once around my left wing. When I beat my wing to shake it off, it bit.

A wing is only a wing while it can push the air. Mine could not. The air slid past it, and I was falling. I tumbled through the paper kites and the shouting, and I hit the roof among Farah's water pots.

Everyone was looking up at the fight. Only Farah was looking down. She knelt beside me. I hissed at her and opened my beak. She did not run away, and she did not grab me. She took the dupatta from her shoulders and dropped it over me, gently, so that the world went dark and quiet. Through the cloth I felt her small hands hold my wings closed against my body.
'Bilal,' she said, in a voice I had not heard from her. 'Bring scissors. Not your string. Scissors.'

They cut the glass thread away. Then her mother carried me through the crowded lanes, wrapped in pink cloth, to a building full of birds. It was a hospital just for birds, run by kind people in white. There were pigeons with bandaged feet, a parrot with a splint, and three other kites like me, all cut by string.
I stayed there for many weeks. My feathers grew back.

When they let me go, I flew straight to my water tank. It was a hot afternoon in October. Below me, on her roof, Farah was flying the pink kite on plain white cotton thread. It had no glass at all. Bilal stood beside her. He was holding the spool for her, and none of his string glittered.

I stepped off the tank and found a rising bubble of air. Farah looked up, and I am almost sure she knew me. For a long moment we hung there together over the old city. Her kite was held by a string, and I was held by nothing but the way I leaned. We were both doing the same thing. We were pushing the air down, and the air was pushing us up.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Farah's kite fails while she runs along with the wind and lets the string go slack. It flies the moment she stands still with the wind at her back, the kite's face turned into the wind, and pulls the string tight. The wind pushes the kite, the string holds it, and the tilted kite turns that push upwards. The cheel does the same thing without a string, leaning tilted wings on rising warm air. When the glass string damages a wing, the wing can no longer push the air, and it falls. Every flyer in the story stays up the same way: by pushing air downwards.
ask: In the story, Farah's kite would not fly at first. What did she change to make it climb?
Why did the kite rise when Farah pulled the string tight, and sag when the string went slack?
How did the cheel stay up in the sky without flapping?
Why did the cheel fall when the glass string cut a wing?
At the end, Bilal holds a spool of plain cotton string. Why do you think he changed?

games.title: How Does It Fly?

printables.title: 24 flyer cards to cut out
items: Black kite (cheel) circling on a hot day

printables.title: Five playing mats
items: FLAPPERS: moving wings push air down and back
GLIDERS: still wings, sliding slowly down the air
HELD ON A STRING: the wind pushes, the string holds
SPINNERS AND FLOATERS: they fall very slowly
ENGINES AND OTHER TRICKS: propellers, jets, hot air or rockets

rules: Cut out the 24 cards and the 20 feathers. Shuffle the cards and put them face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Put the card on the mat that shows how it stays up. Say why.
Then say what it pushes on to stay up. A hot-air balloon and a rocket do not push on air: say what they do instead. A good answer wins one feather.
Some cards could go on two mats. If you can explain both, win two feathers.
If the feathers run out, keep score on paper.
When the cards run out, the player with the most feathers wins. If feathers are equal, the win is shared.

flow.do: 1. Lay the five mats in a row on the floor. 2. Shuffle the 24 flyer cards and put them face down in a pile. 3. Put the feather tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Everything on these cards flies or floats in the air. But they don't all do it the same way. For each card, we decide how it stays up.
flow.kid: Lay the five mats in a row. Mix up the cards and put them face down. For each card, decide how it stays up.
flow.context: This is the first step of the How Does It Fly? card game. You sort flying things by the trick they use to stay up.

flow.do: Find the card 'Paper plane'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise. A paper plane. Does it flap? Does it have an engine? Which mat does it go on?
flow.kid: Practice card: a paper plane. Does it flap? Does it have an engine? Which mat does it go on?

check.q: A paper plane, after it leaves your hand. Which mat does it go on?
check.why: Gliders is right. Once it leaves your hand, a paper plane has no thrust, so it slides slowly down the air on still wings. Picking FLAPPERS mixes up the throw with flapping. Picking ENGINES counts your arm as an engine, but your arm only pushes for a moment.

ask.q: What does a paper plane push on to stay up?
good: The air.
Its wings push the air down.

flow.do: 1. Take turns drawing a card and placing it on a mat. 2. The player says why, and what it pushes on. 3. Give one feather token for each good answer.
flow.say: Tell me how it stays up, and what it pushes on.
flow.kid: Take turns. Put your card on a mat. Say how it stays up. Each good answer wins a feather.
flow.parent: Tricky cards: a vulture flaps to take off but mostly glides and soars, so they can go on two mats. A helicopter has spinning wings, its blades, which push air down. A hot-air balloon is different. Its hot air is lighter than the cold air around it, so it floats up, like a cork in water. A rocket is different again. It throws hot gas out backwards and needs no air at all. That is why Ingenuity on Mars needed spinning blades, but rockets don't.

flow.do: Look at the ENGINES AND OTHER TRICKS mat together. Ask which of these things could still fly in space.
flow.say: Which of these could still fly in space, where there is no air at all?
flow.kid: Look at the engines mat. Which one could still fly in space, with no air?

check.q: Which of these could still fly in space, where there is no air?
check.why: A rocket is right. It throws hot gas out backwards, and the gas pushes it forwards, with no air needed. Picking the helicopter misses that its blades must push on air. Picking the balloon misses that it floats only because it is lighter than the air around it.

flow.think: Almost every card pushes on air. What does that tell you about air?

flow.do: Count the tokens to find the winner. Then count how many cards landed on each mat.
flow.say: Which mat has the most cards? Which way of flying do you think is the hardest work?
flow.kid: Count your feathers. Who won? Which mat has the most cards? Which way of flying looks like the hardest work?

games.context: This is a card game about the different ways things fly. Players sort 24 flyers, from sparrows to seeds to a helicopter on Mars, by the trick each one uses to stay up.

games.title: Paper Plane Airport

printables.title: A runway mat made of 3 sheets of paper taped in a row
8 pilot challenge cards
items: Add one paper clip to the nose before you throw.
Bend the back edges of the wings up a little.
Tear a small strip off one wing.

rules: Each pilot folds one paper plane.
Put the runway mat on the floor, 3 big steps from the throwing line.
On your turn, take a challenge card and do what it says. Then throw.
Score the sheet your plane comes to rest on. Missing the runway scores 0.
Write the points and what the plane did in the pilot log.
After 4 rounds each, the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Help each player fold a simple dart-shaped paper plane from one A4 sheet. 2. Tape 3 sheets in a row to make the runway. 3. Mark a throwing line 3 big steps away.
flow.say: Every pilot needs a plane and every plane needs a runway. Let's build our airport.
flow.kid: Fold your paper plane. Tape three sheets in a row. That is your runway. Stand 3 big steps away.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paper Plane Airport. It is a landing game. Pilots try to land paper planes on a paper runway on the floor.
flow.parent: To fold a simple dart plane, first fold the sheet in half the long way and open it. Fold the two top corners to the middle line. Fold the new slanted edges to the middle again. Fold the plane in half. Last, fold down each wing.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each pilot draws a challenge card, does it, then throws. 2. Score the landing. 3. Write it in the pilot log.
flow.say: What did that card do to your plane? Did it climb, dive or glide?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Do what it says. Throw your plane. Did it climb, dive or glide? Write your points.

ask.q: What did the paper clip on the nose do?
good: It stopped the plane swooping up and dropping.
It made the nose heavier, so it flew steadier.

ask.q: What did bending up the back edges of the wings do?
good: The nose went up.
It glided further.
It swooped up if I bent them too much.

flow.parent: A paper clip on the nose moves the plane's balance point forward. That usually makes it steadier. Bending up the back edges of the wings pushes the tail down and the nose up. Too much, and the plane swoops up and stalls. Tearing a wing makes it roll to one side.

flow.do: Ask each pilot which change helped most. Try that change again to check.
flow.say: Which change helped most? Let's try it once more, to check it wasn't luck.
flow.kid: Which change helped your plane most? Try it again. Was it luck, or does it work every time?

check.q: A paper plane swoops up, stops and drops. What is the best fix?
options: Add a paper clip to the nose
Bend the back edges of the wings up more
check.why: Adding a paper clip to the nose is right. It moves the balance point forward, so the plane glides instead of swooping. Picking 'throw it harder' makes the swoop steeper. Picking 'bend the back edges up more' lifts the nose even more, so it stalls sooner.

flow.do: Add up the points and find the winner. Read out the best 'What the plane did' notes.
flow.say: Real pilots learn by trying, noticing and changing one thing at a time. So did you.
flow.kid: Add up your points. Who won? Real pilots learn by changing one thing at a time.
flow.think: Why is it better to change only one thing before each throw?

games.context: This is a paper plane landing game. Pilot challenge cards make players change their planes, so everyone learns what makes a plane climb, dive or glide.

experiments.title: The Paper Clip Pilot: does weight on the nose help a plane fly further?
experiments.question: Does adding paper clips to the nose of a paper plane make it fly further?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Which will fly furthest: the plane with no clip, with 1 clip, or with 3 clips on its nose? And why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same plane each time and throw it from the same line, with the same gentle throw. Change only the number of clips. Throw each one 3 times, because one throw can be a fluke.

materials.item: one sheet of A4 paper, folded into a dart plane
3 paper clips
a measuring tape, or a 1-metre string with knots every 10 cm (lay it end to end to measure longer throws)
a pencil, the results table and a long hallway or a terrace

experiments.safety: Never throw planes towards anyone's face.

schedule.what: Guess. Throw the plane 3 times with no clip, 1 clip and 3 clips. Measure. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each plane. Make each bar as tall as its middle distance.

flow.do: 1. Help your child fold one dart plane. 2. Stick a strip of tape on the floor as the throwing line. 3. Ask your child to guess which version will fly furthest.
flow.say: We'll test one plane three ways. No clips, one clip and three clips on its nose. Which do you think will fly furthest?
flow.kid: Fold one paper plane. Mark a line on the floor. Guess. Will no clip, 1 clip or 3 clips fly furthest?

good: The clip makes it heavier, so it falls faster.
The clip makes it steadier.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Clip Pilot experiment. You find out whether weight on a paper plane's nose helps it fly further.

flow.do: 1. Throw the plane with no clip, gently and level, 3 times. 2. After each throw, measure from the line to where it stopped. 3. Write each distance in the table.
flow.say: Same gentle throw every time. Let's measure each one and write it down.
flow.kid: Throw the plane gently and level, 3 times. Measure each throw from the line. Write it down.
flow.parent: Keep the throw the same each time. Let the same person throw. If one throw goes badly wrong, like hitting a wall, throw it again. To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one.

flow.do: 1. Clip 1 paper clip to the nose. Throw and measure 3 times. 2. Now add 2 more clips, so there are 3. Throw and measure 3 times.
flow.say: Watch how the plane flies, not just how far. Does it swoop, dive or glide?
flow.kid: Put 1 clip on the nose. Throw 3 times and measure. Now try 3 clips. Watch how it flies.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values, one bar for each plane.
flow.say: Each plane gets one bar. The taller the bar, the further it flew.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each plane. Make it as tall as its middle number. Taller means further.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how far each plane flew (middle of 3 throws)
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: In the made-up example chart, the plane with 1 clip flew furthest. Why might 1 clip fly further than no clip?
options: The clip moves the balance point forward, so the plane glides steadily instead of swooping
The clip pushes the air down
check.why: The clip moves the balance point forward, so the plane glides steadily. Picking 'heavier things always fly further' doesn't fit the example chart, because 3 clips flew the shortest distance. Picking 'the clip pushes the air down' mixes up the clip with the wings, which do the pushing.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. Your results may be different, and that is fine. One clip does not always help, and an honest 'it made no difference' is a real result. A good answer sounds like this, with made-up numbers. What I think: one clip on the nose helps the plane fly furthest. What I saw: with no clip it swooped up and dropped at about 4 metres. With 1 clip it glided to 6 metres. With 3 clips it dived down at 3 metres. Why: the clip moves the balance point forward, so the plane flies steadily. Too much weight makes it dive.

experiments.context: In this experiment you throw the same paper plane with no clip, one clip and three clips on its nose. You measure how far it flies each time.

experiments.title: Seed Spinners: do longer wings fall more slowly?
experiments.question: Does a paper spinner with longer wings take longer to fall?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Will the spinner with short wings, middle wings or long wings take longest to fall? And why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same paper and the same paper clip on each spinner. Drop each one from the same height, about 2 metres, by letting go, not throwing. Change only the wing length. Time each one 3 times, because one drop can be a fluke.

materials.item: 3 strips of paper, each 4 cm wide, cut 22 cm, 19 cm and 16 cm long
a ruler
scissors
3 paper clips
a phone stopwatch
a measuring tape, or a door: most doors are about 2 metres high

experiments.safety: A grown-up holds the spinner as high as they can reach. Never drop things from a balcony.

schedule.what: Make 3 spinners with short, middle and long wings. Drop each 3 times from 2 metres and time it.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart of the middle times, one bar for each spinner.

setup.caption: 1. Cut the top of a paper strip into two wings. Fold the bottom and add a clip.

setup.art: The two wings folded in opposite directions, one forward and one back, like a T.
setup.caption: 2. Fold one wing forward and one wing back.

setup.art: A grown-up on a step holding the spinner up high next to a wall marked at 2 metres.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up holds it 2 metres up.

setup.art: The spinner whirling down while a child on the floor watches a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 4. Let go, and time the fall.

setup.art: Three spinners side by side, with short, middle and long wings.
setup.caption: 5. Test spinners with short, middle and long wings.

flow.do: 1. Cut 3 paper strips, each 4 cm wide. Make them 22 cm, 19 cm and 16 cm long. 2. On each strip, mark 12 cm up from the bottom. That part is the body. 3. Cut down the middle from the top to the mark. That makes two wings, 10 cm, 7 cm or 4 cm long. 4. Fold the bottom of each body up twice and add one clip. 5. Fold one wing forward and one wing back.
flow.say: These are model mahogany seeds. Real winged seeds spin as they fall. Which one do you think will fall slowest?
flow.kid: Make three paper spinners: short wings, middle wings and long wings. Fold one wing forward and one back. Guess which falls slowest.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Seed Spinners experiment. You make paper models of spinning winged seeds, like mahogany seeds.
flow.parent: Keep the body the same length and use one clip each. Only the wings should change. Before you start, stick a piece of tape on a wall or a door at 2 metres. If you can't reach it, use the highest height you can, and keep it the same for every drop.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up holds a spinner by its clip, 2 metres above the floor. 2. Say 'Go' and let it drop. 3. The child starts the stopwatch on 'Go' and stops it when the spinner lands. 4. Do this 3 times for each spinner and write down each time.
flow.say: Ready? Go! Stop the timer the moment it touches the floor.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to hold the spinner up high. Start the timer when they say Go. Stop it when it lands. Do each one 3 times.

ask.q: What does the spinner do as it falls?
good: It spins round.
It falls slowly, like a real seed.

flow.parent: A paper spinner takes only 1 or 2 seconds to fall 2 metres, so the times are short. A phone stopwatch shows tenths of a second, like 1.6. Read it as 'one point six seconds'. If a spinner hits a wall or tumbles, drop it again.

flow.do: Find the middle time for each spinner. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each.
flow.say: Put the three times in order and take the middle one. Then draw the bars.
flow.kid: Find the middle time for each spinner. Draw a bar for each one. Taller means slower.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how long each paper spinner took to fall 2 metres
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: In the Seed Spinners test, a tall bar means the spinner…
check.why: A tall bar means the spinner took longest to fall. The bars show seconds, so taller means slower. Picking 'fell fastest' is a common mix-up, because tall bars often mean 'best' or 'fastest'. Always read the label on the side of the chart.

flow.do: Take the clip off one spinner and drop it. Then put two clips on it and drop it.
flow.say: What happens with no clip? And with two?
flow.kid: Take off the clip and drop it. Now try two clips. What changed?
flow.think: In a real mahogany fruit, the heavy seed sits at one end and the wing is at the other. Why might that help the seed spin?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: longer wings make a spinner fall more slowly. What I saw: the short wings took about 1.2 seconds to fall 2 metres, and the long wings took about 2.2 seconds. Why: longer wings sweep through more air as they spin. So they can push enough air down to hold up the clip while falling more slowly.

experiments.context: In this experiment you make paper spinners, like the winged seeds of a mahogany tree. You drop them from 2 metres and time how long each one takes to fall.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how long each paper spinner took to fall 2 metres
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

experiments.title: Hand Wing: how does tilt change the push of the air?
experiments.question: When moving air meets a flat hand or a card, how does tilting it change the push?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Will a flat hand, a slightly tilted hand or a steeply tilted hand be pushed up the most? And why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep the fan on the same speed. Hold your hand at the same distance from it each time. Change only the tilt.
results_table: Push upwards: none, a little or a lot
Push backwards: none, a little or a lot

materials.item: a table fan with a safety guard, on a low table, set to its fastest speed
a postcard or a piece of card about the size of your palm

experiments.safety: A grown-up switches the fan on and off. Fingers stay well outside the fan's guard, at least an arm's length from it.

schedule.what: Hold a flat hand in front of a fan at three tilts. Feel the push. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with words. Then draw your hand at the tilt that got the most push upwards.

setup.art: A table fan with a guard on a low table, a grown-up's hand on the switch.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up switches on the fan.

setup.art: A child's hand held flat, palm down, an arm's length in front of the fan.
setup.caption: 2. Hold your hand flat, an arm's length away.

setup.art: The same hand with its front edge, the fingertips, tilted up a little, an up arrow above it.
setup.caption: 3. Tilt the front edge up a little.

setup.art: The hand tilted up steeply, nearly upright, with a big back arrow and wobble lines.
setup.caption: 4. Tilt it up steeply.

flow.do: 1. Put the fan on a low table and switch it on at its fastest speed. 2. Your child holds one hand flat, palm down, fingers together and pointing at the fan, an arm's length away from it.
flow.say: Your hand is a wing now. The fan is the wind. Hold it flat. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to switch on the fan. Hold your hand flat, an arm's length away. Your hand is a wing! What do you feel?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hand Wing experiment. You hold your hand in front of a fan and feel how the air pushes it.
flow.parent: The air from a table fan is slow, so the push on a hand is gentle. Ask your child to relax their arm and close their eyes to feel it. The card in the next steps shows the push more clearly.

flow.do: 1. Slowly tilt the front edge of the hand up a little. 2. Then tilt it up steeply, nearly upright. 3. After each tilt, write down the push upwards, the push backwards, and whether it was steady.
flow.say: Tilt the front of your hand up, just a little. Now tilt it right up. Which way is it pushed each time?
flow.kid: Tilt the front of your hand up a little. Feel it lift? Now tilt it right up. What happens now? Write it down.

ask.q: When was your hand pushed up the most?
good: When it was tilted a little.
Not flat, and not too steep.

flow.parent: With a slight tilt, the hand is pushed up a little. This is lift. With a steep tilt, the hand is mostly pushed back and starts to wobble. Real wings do this too. It is called a stall.

flow.do: 1. Hold the card loosely by one short edge, between finger and thumb, so it hangs straight down. 2. Hold it an arm's length in front of the fan, with the hanging card facing the fan. 3. Watch what the moving air does to it.
flow.say: The card hangs straight down. What do you think the moving air will do to it? Why?
flow.kid: Hold the card loosely by its top edge. Let it hang down. Hold it in front of the fan. Watch it.
flow.parent: The air pushes the card back, so it swings up into a slant, like a kite on a string. The slanted card turns the air downwards, and the air holds it up. If your fan has a slower speed, try it. The card then hangs more steeply, because slower air pushes less.

check.q: In the Hand Wing test, when does the air push your hand up the most?
options: When its front edge is tilted up a little
When it is tilted up steeply
check.why: A little tilt is right. It turns the moving air downwards, so the air pushes the hand up. Picking 'flat' misses that a flat hand hardly turns the air. Picking 'steeply' misses that a steep hand is mostly pushed back and wobbles. That is a stall.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a wing tilted up a little gets the most lift. What I saw: flat, my hand was hardly pushed up. Tilted a little, it was pushed up a lot. Tilted steeply, it was pushed back and wobbled. Why: a little tilt turns the air downwards, so the air pushes my hand up. Too much tilt and the air tumbles.

experiments.context: In this experiment you hold your flat hand in front of a fan at different tilts. You feel how the air pushes it up, or back.
