activities.title: Air Is Real: the dry tissue and the cardboard run

materials.item: a clear glass, a tissue, and a bucket or big bowl of water
a big flat piece of cardboard, or an open umbrella

schedule.what: Show that air takes up space and pushes back.

activities.record: Draw the glass in the water, with the air and the dry tissue inside it.

setup.art: A tissue pushed tightly into the bottom of a clear glass.
setup.caption: 1. Push a tissue into the bottom of a glass.

setup.art: The glass held upside down and pushed straight down into a bucket of water, a pocket of air visible inside.
setup.caption: 2. Push the glass straight down into the water, upside down.

setup.art: The glass lifted out and the tissue pulled out, completely dry.
setup.caption: 3. Lift it straight out. Feel the tissue.

setup.art: A child running across a terrace holding a big flat cardboard sheet in front, with air arrows pushing back.
setup.caption: 4. Run holding a big card flat in front of you.

flow.do: 1. Push a tissue into the bottom of a dry glass, so it stays when the glass is turned over. 2. Turn the glass upside down. 3. Push it straight down into the water, all the way under. 4. Lift it straight up and pull out the tissue.
flow.say: Is this glass empty? Let's find out. Watch the tissue.
flow.kid: Push a tissue into a glass. Turn it upside down. Push it straight into the water. Lift it out. Is the tissue wet?

ask.q: Why did the tissue stay dry?
good: Air in the glass kept the water out.
The glass was full of air.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Air Is Real activity. You show that an 'empty' glass is really full of air.

flow.do: 1. Go to the longest clear space you have, like a hallway, a terrace or a park. 2. Your child runs holding a big flat card in front of them, facing forwards. 3. Then they run holding it edge-on, like a knife.
flow.say: Which way was harder to run? Something pushed back on the card. What was it?
flow.kid: Run holding the card flat in front of you. Now run holding it edge-on. Which was harder? What pushed back?

check.q: In the Air Is Real activity, running with the card held flat was harder. Why?
options: The air pushed back on the card
check.why: The air pushed back on the card. A flat card pushes against lots of air, so lots of air pushes back. Picking 'the card got heavier' misses that it was the same card both times. Picking 'the floor was rough' misses that your feet were the same both times. Only the card changed.

flow.do: Talk together about how wings use this push.
flow.say: Air is a real material. It pushes back. A wing is a clever way of using that push to hold something up.
flow.kid: Air is a real material. It pushes back. Wings use that push to stay up!
flow.think: If air pushes back so hard on a card, how hard must it push on the wings of a big plane?

activities.context: This activity shows that air is a real material. It fills an 'empty' glass, and it pushes back when you run with a card.

activities.title: Float a Feather, Float a Ball (hair dryer)

materials.item: a hair dryer with a cool or low-heat setting
a light feather, a ping-pong ball and a small balloon

activities.safety: A grown-up holds the hair dryer and uses the cool setting. Keep it away from water and from hair.

schedule.what: Float a feather and a ping-pong ball on a stream of air.

activities.record: Draw the ball floating in the air stream. Draw arrows showing the air.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a hair dryer pointing straight up, switched to the cool setting.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up points the dryer straight up, on cool.

setup.art: A feather floating and fluttering above the dryer.
setup.caption: 2. Let go of a feather above it.

setup.art: A ping-pong ball hovering steadily a hand's width above the dryer.
setup.caption: 3. Now let go of a ping-pong ball above it.

setup.art: The dryer tilted to one side, the ball still hanging in the slanted air stream.
setup.caption: 4. Slowly tilt the dryer.

flow.do: 1. Switch the dryer to cool and point it straight up. 2. Let your child hold a feather above it and let go.
flow.say: Let go of the feather. What is holding it up?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to hold the dryer, on cool. Let go of a feather above it. What holds it up?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Float a Feather activity. You use a stream of moving air to hold up light things.
flow.parent: A feather is light and flutters about, and may blow away. The ping-pong ball hovers more steadily, so start with the ball if the feather will not stay.

flow.do: 1. Let go of a ping-pong ball a hand's width above the dryer. 2. Watch it hover. 3. Slowly tilt the dryer to one side. 4. Try a small blown-up balloon.
flow.say: The ball stays in the stream, even when we tilt it. Why doesn't it fall out?
flow.kid: Let go of a ping-pong ball above the dryer. It floats! Now tilt the dryer slowly. Does the ball fall out?

ask.q: What happens when the ball drifts to the edge of the air stream?
good: It moves back into the middle.
The air pushes it back.

flow.parent: The air pushes the ball up, like a hand. When the ball drifts to one edge, the fast air curves around it. Then the ball is pushed back into the stream. Many books explain this with Bernoulli's rule, that fast air pushes less on things beside it. Scientists argue about the best simple explanation, just as they do for wings.

flow.do: Talk about how the air held things up, and compare it with a wing.
flow.say: The dryer pushes air up to hold the ball. A wing does the opposite. It pushes air down, so the air pushes the wing up.
flow.kid: The dryer pushes air up, and it holds the ball up. A wing pushes air down. Then the air pushes the wing up.

check.q: In the hair dryer activity, what holds the ping-pong ball up?
options: The dryer pulls it like a magnet
Nothing, it is too light to fall
check.why: Moving air holds the ball up, by pushing on it from below. Picking 'pulls it like a magnet' gives the dryer a pull it doesn't have. It only blows. Picking 'too light to fall' misses that the ball drops as soon as the dryer is switched off.

activities.context: In this activity a grown-up points a hair dryer upwards. You float a feather and a ping-pong ball on the moving air, and see the air push.

activities.title: Flying Seed Hunt

materials.item: a paper bag or envelope for seeds, and a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Go with a grown-up. Wash your hands after. Don't put seeds in your mouth. Aak plant sap stings eyes, so collect only the dry fluffy seeds, never break the plant.

schedule.what: Hunt for flying seeds in a park or along a tree-lined road, then test-drop them at home.

activities.record: Stick or draw each seed. Write how they fly: parachute, spinner or glider. Time how long each takes to fall from your head height.

setup.art: A child and grown-up under a big-leaf mahogany tree, picking up winged seeds from the pavement.
setup.caption: 1. Look under big trees for seeds with wings.

setup.art: Silky white fluff bursting from a dry aak pod on a roadside bush.
setup.caption: 2. Look for fluffy seeds on bushes and in the air.

setup.art: A table at home with seeds sorted into three groups: fluffy, spinning wing, flat glider.
setup.caption: 3. Sort your seeds at home.

setup.art: A child standing, dropping a winged seed from head height while another child watches a timer.
setup.caption: 4. Drop each one from head height and time it.

flow.do: 1. Walk under big trees in a park or along a road. 2. Look on the ground for seeds with wings or fluff. 3. Collect as many kinds as you can.
flow.say: We're seed detectives. We're looking for seeds that fly. Look for wings, fluff and spinners.
flow.kid: You are a seed detective! Look under trees for seeds with wings or fluff. Collect as many kinds as you can.
flow.parent: This hunt needs a park or a road with big trees. Good finds in Indian towns: winged big-leaf mahogany seeds under avenue trees, mostly from February to May. Silky fluff from aak bushes, found most of the year, and from semal trees in March and April. Drumstick seeds, with three papery wings, inside dry drumstick pods. Sal and arjun fruits have wings too. If you find none, use the paper spinners from the Seed Spinners experiment instead.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Flying Seed Hunt. You look for seeds that travel through the air, on parachutes, wings or spinners.

flow.do: 1. At home, sort the seeds into three groups: parachutes, spinners and gliders. 2. Drop each one from head height. 3. Time how long it takes to land.
flow.say: Which kind falls slowest? Which do you think travels furthest on a windy day?
flow.kid: Sort your seeds: parachutes, spinners and gliders. Drop each one. Time how long it takes to land.

check.q: In the Flying Seed Hunt, a mahogany seed spins while falling. Which kind of flying seed is this?
check.why: A spinner is right. The single wing makes mahogany seeds whirl as they fall, which slows them down. Picking 'a parachute' mixes them up with fluffy seeds like aak and dandelion. Picking 'doesn't fly' misses that they fall slowly enough for the wind to carry them.

flow.do: Talk about why plants send seeds so far.
flow.say: Why is it good for a tree if the seeds fly far away, instead of dropping just underneath?
flow.kid: Why is it good for a tree if the seeds fly far away?
flow.think: Some seeds fly, some float on water, and some stick to animals' fur. If you were a plant, which way would you send your seeds?

activities.context: This is a seed hunt, if you have a park or a tree-lined road nearby. You collect seeds that fly, sort them by how they fly, and time how slowly they fall.

activities.title: Bird Watch: flap, glide or soar?

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
binoculars, if you have them
a phone stopwatch

activities.safety: Watch from a safe rooftop with a railing, a balcony or a park, with a grown-up. Never look at the Sun, with or without binoculars.

schedule.what: Watch birds for 12 minutes. Tally which birds flap, glide or soar. Count wingbeats.

activities.record: Make a tally table with three columns: flapping, gliding and soaring. Write which birds you saw doing each.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up on a terrace with a railing, the child holding a notebook with a three-column tally table.
setup.caption: 1. Find a safe place to watch the sky.

setup.art: A pigeon flapping fast across the sky, wings blurred.
setup.caption: 2. Watch a bird flap. Count their wingbeats for 10 seconds.

setup.art: Black kites circling high in the midday sky without flapping.
setup.caption: 3. Look high up for birds circling without flapping.

setup.art: A tally table with marks in the columns flapping, gliding and soaring.
setup.caption: 4. Make a tally mark for each bird you see.

flow.do: Draw a tally table with three columns: flapping, gliding and soaring. Explain each word.
flow.say: Flapping means wings beating. Gliding means wings held still, sinking slowly. Soaring means wings still, and the bird rising or staying up in circles.
flow.kid: Draw a table with three columns: flapping, gliding and soaring. Make a tally mark for each bird you see.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bird Watch. You watch the sky and sort birds by how they are flying: flapping, gliding or soaring.

flow.do: 1. Watch the sky for 12 minutes, from a window, balcony or terrace. 2. Make a tally mark for each bird you see. 3. Pick one flapping bird and count the wingbeats for 10 seconds.
flow.say: Where are the soaring birds? Look high up. Are they flapping at all?
flow.kid: Watch the sky. Tally each bird. Pick one flapping bird. Count the wingbeats for 10 seconds.
flow.parent: Around midday on hot, sunny days, black kites and sometimes vultures soar in circles. They are riding thermals, rising bubbles of warm air. Crows and pigeons flap more. Small birds, like sparrows, flap fast and then fold their wings for a moment, which saves energy. If no bird soars while you watch, tally what you do see.

ask.q: Why do you think the soaring birds go round in circles?
good: To stay inside the rising warm air.
The warm air is in one place, so they circle in it.

flow.do: Count the tallies together. Talk about which way of flying looks easiest.
flow.say: Which kind of flying did we see most? Which kind looks like the least work?
flow.kid: Count your tally marks. Which kind of flying did you see most? Which looks easiest?
flow.think: Soaring birds use the Sun's heat to climb, without flapping. Where else does the Sun's heat make air or water move?

activities.context: This is a bird-watching activity. You watch the sky for about 12 minutes and sort birds by how they fly: flapping, gliding or soaring.

activities.title: Be the Air (act it out)

materials.item: a big piece of cardboard, about as wide as your arms, to be the wing
2 or more people: one holds the wing and the others are air molecules (soft toys can join in)

schedule.what: Act out air molecules bumping into a wing.

activities.record: Draw the tilted wing, the air molecules hitting its underside and being steered down, and an arrow for the push up on the wing.

setup.art: Three children standing in a room, each pretending to be a zooming air molecule.
setup.caption: 1. Everyone except one is an air molecule.

setup.art: A grown-up walking slowly forward holding a big cardboard wing tilted up at the front.
setup.caption: 2. One person walks slowly with a tilted cardboard wing.

setup.art: Children gently bumping into the underside of the cardboard and being pushed downwards.
setup.caption: 3. Molecules bump into the underside and get pushed down.

flow.do: 1. Everyone except one person becomes an air molecule. 2. Molecules walk quickly around the room in straight lines, changing direction when they meet something.
flow.say: Air is made of tiny molecules, zooming about and bumping into everything. You are the molecules. Zoom around, gently!
flow.kid: You are an air molecule! Walk fast in straight lines. When you bump into something, change direction.
flow.context: This is the first step of Be the Air. It is a short play where people act as air molecules and a cardboard sheet acts as a wing.

flow.do: 1. The wing-holder walks slowly through the room, holding the cardboard tilted up at the front. 2. Molecules that meet the underside bump it gently and are steered downwards. 3. Swap roles so everyone holds the wing.
flow.say: Wing-holder, can you feel the bumps underneath pushing your wing up? Molecules, which way does the wing send you?
flow.kid: Bump gently into the bottom of the wing. Which way does the wing send you? Holding the wing? Feel the bumps push it up!
flow.parent: This is a model. Real molecules are far tinier and faster, and a real wing meets countless numbers of them. The key idea is right. The tilted wing pushes molecules down, and the molecules push the wing up.

flow.do: Talk about what the play showed.
flow.say: The wing pushed the molecules down. The molecules pushed the wing up. That push is lift.
flow.kid: The wing pushed you down. You pushed the wing up. That push is called lift!

check.q: In the Be the Air play, which way did the tilted wing send the air molecules?
check.why: Downwards is right. The tilted wing pushed the molecules down, and they pushed the wing up. That is lift. Picking 'upwards' turns the picture over. Picking 'nowhere' misses that every bump changed a molecule's direction.

flow.think: You can't see a single air molecule. How did scientists ever find out they exist?

activities.context: This is a short play. People act as air molecules, and someone walks through them with a tilted cardboard wing. It shows what lift is deep down.

activities.title: Wings Dance and Wind Breath

materials.item: a dupatta or a light scarf for each person
some open space, and music if you like
a small feather or a scrap of tissue for each person

schedule.what: Dance the five ways of flying, then do a calm breathing exercise.

activities.record: Draw your favourite flying move. Label it flapping, gliding, soaring, spinning or floating.

setup.art: A child with arms wide holding a dupatta like wings, beating them up and down.
setup.caption: 1. Flap like a crow.

setup.art: The child leaning forward, arms still and wide, gliding across the room.
setup.caption: 2. Glide like a paper plane.

setup.art: The child turning slowly in a big circle, arms tilted, rising onto tiptoes.
setup.caption: 3. Soar in circles like a cheel.

setup.art: The child sitting cross-legged, eyes closed, breathing out slowly onto a feather on their palm.
setup.caption: 4. Breathe out slowly, like a gentle wind.

flow.do: 1. Each person holds a dupatta like wings. 2. Call out a way of flying, and everyone dances it. Flap like a crow. Glide like a paper plane. Soar in circles like a cheel. Spin down like a mahogany seed. Float like aak fluff.
flow.say: When I call a word, move like that flyer. Flap! Glide! Soar! Spin! Float!
flow.kid: Hold your dupatta like wings. When you hear a word, move like that flyer. Flap! Glide! Soar! Spin! Float!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wings Dance. You dance the different ways that birds, planes and seeds fly.

ask.q: Which dance move was the most tiring? Why?
good: Flapping, because you have to keep moving your arms.
Spinning, because you get dizzy.

flow.do: 1. Sit down together. 2. Each person puts a small feather or a scrap of tissue on their palm. 3. Breathe in slowly through the nose. 4. Breathe out very gently through the mouth, so the feather just trembles but does not blow away.
flow.say: Breathe in slowly. Now breathe out so gently that the feather only trembles. You are the wind now.
flow.kid: Put a feather on your hand. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out so gently the feather only trembles. You are the wind!

flow.do: End the dance by asking which flyer each person liked being most.
flow.say: Which flyer did you like being most? Why?
flow.kid: Which flyer did you like being most? Tell someone why.

check.q: In the Wings Dance, which move was soaring?
options: Turning slowly in big circles with your arms still
Spinning on the spot as you sink down
check.why: Turning slowly in big circles with still arms is soaring, like a cheel in a thermal. Flapping fast is flapping, like a crow. Spinning as you sink is the mahogany seed's trick.

flow.think: People have danced like birds for thousands of years. Why do you think flying makes people want to dance?

activities.context: This is a dance and breathing activity. You move like the different flyers in this unit, and then breathe out gently like the wind.

projects.title: Build and Fly a Patang

materials.item: kite paper or tissue paper, about 50 cm square
2 thin bamboo sticks, or 2 long bamboo skewers taped end to end, about 50 cm and 45 cm
glue, tape and scissors
plain cotton kite thread on a spool, never glass-coated manja
a long strip of old cloth or newspaper for a tail

projects.safety: Only a grown-up cuts bamboo. Fly in an open park or a rooftop with a high railing and a grown-up, far from electricity wires. Never use glass-coated manja, which cuts hands and birds. If the kite catches on a wire, let it go.

schedule.what: Make the frame, cover it with paper and leave the glue to dry.
Add the tail and the string loop, called the bridle. Decorate the kite.
Fly the kite. Change the tail and the tilt to make it fly better.

projects.record: Draw your kite and label the sticks, the paper, the bridle and the tail. Write what you changed on Day 3 and what happened.

setup.art: Two bamboo sticks crossed and tied into a cross shape, the shorter one across the top third of the longer one.
setup.caption: 1. Tie two sticks into a cross.

setup.art: The cross laid on a sheet of tissue paper, the paper cut into a diamond with a 2 cm border folded and glued over the sticks.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the frame with paper.

setup.art: A finished diamond kite with a string loop tied from the top to the bottom, and a long cloth tail.
setup.caption: 3. Add a string loop and a tail.

setup.art: A child in a park facing the wind with a tight string, the kite rising behind a helper who has just let go.
setup.caption: 4. Face the wind, keep the string tight, and let it rise.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up trims the sticks if needed. 2. Lay the shorter stick across the longer one, about a third of the way from the top. 3. Tie them tightly with thread, crossing it many times, and add a dab of glue.
flow.say: Every kite needs a light, stiff frame. This cross will be its skeleton.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the sticks. Cross the short one over the long one, near the top. Tie them tight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Build and Fly a Patang project. Over 3 days you make a paper kite and fly it.

flow.do: 1. Tie a thread tightly from tip to tip around the four ends of the cross, to make a diamond outline. 2. Lay the frame on the paper. 3. Cut the paper into a diamond, 2 cm bigger than the outline all round. 4. Fold the 2 cm edges over the thread and glue them down. 5. Leave it to dry overnight.
flow.say: The paper is the kite's wing. It needs to be tight and light.
flow.kid: Tie a thread around the tips of the cross. Cut the paper into a diamond, a bit bigger. Fold the edges over the thread. Glue them. Leave it to dry.
flow.wait: Leave the glue to dry overnight.

flow.do: 1. Tie a string loop, called a bridle, from the top of the long stick to the bottom. 2. Tie the flying thread to the bridle about a third of the way down from the top. 3. Tie a tail, 1 to 2 metres long, to the bottom. 4. Decorate the kite.
flow.say: The bridle sets the tilt. The tail keeps the nose pointing into the wind.
flow.kid: Tie a string loop from top to bottom. Tie the flying string to it, near the top. Add a long tail. Decorate it!
flow.parent: Where the flying string joins the bridle sets the kite's tilt. If the kite will not climb, move the knot a little up or down the bridle and try again. Change it only a little each time.

flow.do: 1. Go to an open space with a steady breeze. 2. The flyer stands still with the wind blowing on their back. 3. A helper (the grown-up, if there are only two of you) carries the kite 10 big steps away, downwind, and holds it up with its face to the wind. 4. On 'Now', the helper lets go and the flyer pulls the string in steadily. 5. Let out string slowly as it climbs, but never let it go slack.
flow.say: The wind pushes the kite. The string holds it back. Keep it tight, and the kite has nowhere to go but up.
flow.kid: Go to an open space with a grown-up. A helper holds the kite up. On 'Now', pull the string. Keep it tight!

ask.q: What happened when the string went slack?
good: The kite started to fall.
It sagged and tumbled.

check.q: In the kite project, your kite spins round and round in the air. What should you try first?
check.why: A longer tail is right. It adds drag at the back and keeps the kite's nose pointing into the wind. Picking 'let the string go slack' makes the kite sag and tumble. Picking 'cut the tail off' usually makes the spinning worse.

flow.do: Change one thing and fly again: a longer tail, a shorter tail, or moving the knot on the bridle. Write what happened.

flow.kid: Change one thing: the tail, or where the string is tied. Fly again. Better or worse? Write it down.

challenges.title: The Slowest Seed
challenges.problem: Design a paper seed that takes as long as possible to fall 2 metres. The longer it stays in the air, the further the wind could carry it.
constraints: Use only half a sheet of A4 paper, tape and one paper clip.
The paper clip is the 'seed'. Your design must carry it.
It must be dropped, not thrown, from 2 metres.
materials: half a sheet of A4 paper
a phone stopwatch and a measuring tape
general: A spinner with long wings, like a mahogany seed.
A parachute: a paper cone or a square with the clip hanging under it, like a dandelion.
A flat glider with the clip at the front, like a Javan cucumber seed.
creative: Cut a fringe of thin strips, like dandelion bristles, so air can flow through.
Give a spinner three wings instead of two, like a drumstick seed.
Curl the wing edges slightly, the way real seed wings curve.

items.p: What does a flying bird push on to stay up?
opts: Nothing. Birds are just very light
items.why: A bird's wings push air down, and the air pushes the bird up. Picking 'nothing' usually means air is thought of as empty. But air is a real material that pushes back.
items.art: A crow mid-downstroke with air arrows going down.

items.p: A tissue is pushed into the bottom of a glass. The glass is pushed upside down into water. Why does the tissue stay dry?
opts: Air in the glass keeps the water out
The water is too cold to get in
items.why: The 'empty' glass is full of air, and the air takes up the space. Picking 'waterproof' usually means the child hasn't seen that the air is doing the work. Try a tissue in a glass held the right way up: it gets wet.

items.p: The upward push of the air on a wing is called ____.
items.why: Lift is the push of the air that holds up wings, kites and gliders.

items.p: Match each force on a flying plane to the way it pushes.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Lift pushes up, weight pulls down, thrust pushes forward, and drag pushes back against the movement.

items.p: Why does a kite need its string?
opts: To pull it up into the sky
To hold it back against the wind, so the wind pushes it up
To stop birds from catching it
It doesn't. The string only helps you find it
items.why: The wind pushes the kite, and the string holds it back. The tilted kite turns that push upwards. Picking 'to pull it up' is a common idea, but the string pulls down and forward, never up. Without the string, the kite blows away and tumbles.

items.p: On a day with no wind at all, you can still fly a kite by running.
items.why: True. Running makes the air move past the kite, just as wind does.

items.p: Sort these flyers. Do they flap, or do they glide without flapping?
items.a: see items
items.why: Flappers beat their wings to push air down and back. Gliders hold their wings or skin flaps still and slowly sink.

items.p: Cheels circle high over a city at midday without flapping. What keeps them up?
items.why: Hot ground warms the air above it, and the warm air rises in bubbles. The birds circle inside and are carried up. Picking 'lighter than air' means birds are being mixed up with balloons. Birds are heavier than air. Wings and rising air hold them up.

items.p: Match each seed to how they fly.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Plants have found many ways to fly: parachutes, spinners and gliders all slow the seed's fall so the wind can carry them far.

items.p: Why do many plants make seeds that fly?
opts: So the seeds can travel far from the parent plant, to new ground
To make the parent tree lighter
items.why: A seed that lands under their parent must share light and water. A seed that travels can find space of their own. Picking 'to keep the seeds dry' misses that a flying seed lands in rain and sun like any other. Over a very long time, plants whose seeds travelled further had more young plants growing in new places.

items.p: A paper plane swoops up, stops and drops. What could help?
opts: A paper clip on its nose
items.why: A clip moves the balance point forward, so the plane glides instead of swooping. Picking 'throw harder' is a common idea. But a harder throw makes it swoop up even more steeply.

items.p: A plane's wings would still hold it up in space, where there is no air.
items.why: False. Wings must push on air. In space there is none, so rockets are used instead.

items.p: Your hand is held flat in front of a fan. You tilt the front edge up a little. What do you feel, and why?
items.a: I feel my hand pushed upwards. The tilted hand turns the moving air downwards, so the air pushes my hand up. That push is lift.
items.why: A small tilt turns the air down and gives lift.

items.p: Draw a paper plane flying. Draw four arrows on it: lift, weight, thrust and drag. Label each.
items.a: Lift points up, weight points down, thrust points forward and drag points back.
items.why: Every flying thing has these four forces on it.
items.art: A blank paper plane outline in flight.

items.p: Pooja, a girl in Class 3, says, 'Air is nothing. An empty bottle has nothing in it.' How could you show her she is wrong, using things at home?
items.a: A strong answer describes a test and what it shows. For example: put the lid on an 'empty' bottle and squeeze it. It pushes back, because air is inside. Or push an open bottle, mouth down, into a bucket of water. The water cannot get in until bubbles of air come out.
items.why: Air is a real material. It takes up space and pushes back, even though we can't see it.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi watch birds from a terrace and argue about which bird is the better flyer.

views.says: The crow is better. Crows flap, so they can take off from a wall, fly in any weather, and carry food home.
The cheel is better. Cheels soar on rising warm air, so they can stay up for an hour with hardly any work.

items.ask: Which bird do you think is the better flyer? Give a reason about how they push on the air. Then say one thing your friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a bird and explains how they stay up: flapping pushes air down and back, and soaring uses rising warm air under still wings. It answers back fairly, for example that soaring saves energy but needs sunshine and rising air, while flapping works anywhere but is hard work.
items.why: Both are good at different jobs. Flapping is strong but tiring. Soaring is cheap but needs thermals, so cheels soar most around midday.

items.p: Look at the chart of the Paper Clip Pilot results. Which plane flew furthest?
items.why: The tallest bar is the plane with 1 clip, at 6 metres. Picking 3 clips usually means 'more weight is better'. Too much weight on the nose makes the plane dive.
items.context: In the Paper Clip Pilot experiment, you throw one paper plane with 0, 1 and 3 clips on its nose. You measure how far it flies.

items.p: Look at the chart of the Seed Spinners results. Which spinner took longest to fall?
items.why: The long-wing spinner has the tallest bar, at 2.2 seconds. Its longer wings sweep through more air, so it can be held up while falling more slowly. Picking 'short wings' often means a tall bar was read as 'fast'. Here a tall bar means slow.

items.p: In the Seed Spinners test, you take the paper clip off a spinner. What will most likely happen?
opts: It tumbles and flutters instead of spinning steadily
items.why: The clip keeps the heavy end at the bottom, so the wings spin evenly. Real winged seeds carry their heavy seed at one end in the same way. Picking 'falls faster' is a fair guess, since it is lighter. But without the weight it doesn't spin well, so it flutters about.
items.context: In the Seed Spinners experiment, you make paper spinners like winged seeds. You drop them from 2 metres and time how long each takes to fall.

items.p: Put the steps for flying a kite in order.
items: Stand still with the wind on your back.
A helper carries the kite away, downwind, and holds it up.
On 'Now', the helper lets go and you pull the string.
Let out string slowly as the kite climbs, keeping it tight.
items.a: order shown
items.why: The kite must face the wind with the string tight from the start. Then it climbs.

items.p: Sort these into what makes flying easier and what makes it harder for a bird.
items: a wet, heavy coat of feathers
items.a: see items
items.why: Light bones, strong muscles, good feathers and rising air all help. Extra weight and damaged feathers make flying harder.

items.p: Paper planes have flat wings, so they can't make any lift.
items.why: False. A flat wing tilted a little still turns air down, so it gets lift. That is why paper planes fly.

items.p: If all of a plane's engines stop high in the sky, the plane falls straight down like a stone.
items.why: False. Engines give thrust, the forward push. The wings give lift. With the engines off, the pilot points the nose a little down, so the plane keeps moving forward and the wings keep pushing air down. It glides, slowly sinking, like a paper plane. In 1983 a Canadian plane ran out of fuel high in the sky and glided safely to a runway.

items.p: Flying squirrels glide from tree to tree. Why can't they keep flying upwards like birds?
opts: They have no flapping wings, so they have no thrust. They can only glide down
items.why: A glider makes lift, but nothing pushes them forward. So they must slowly sink to keep moving. Picking 'too heavy' often means weight is thought to be the only thing that matters. Many birds weigh more than flying squirrels and still fly.

items.p: Why do you think a dandelion seed falls so slowly? Use the word air in your answer.
items.a: The tuft of fine hairs catches the air, so the air pushes up on the seed as the seed falls. Scientists found that air flowing through the hairs makes a swirling ring of air that holds the seed up.
items.why: The tuft slows the fall by pushing on lots of air.

items.p: A kite is flying on a windy day. Show the forces on it, with one arrow for each.
items.why: In this picture the wind blows from left to right. Lift pushes the kite up, its weight pulls it down, the wind pushes it back, and the string pulls it down and forward, towards the flyer.

items.p: After a plane takes off, the wheels fold up inside the plane. Flying crows tuck their feet in close to their bodies too. Why do both do this?
items.a: A strong answer says that wheels and feet sticking out push on the air as the flyer moves, so they make drag, the push of the air backwards. Tucking them in makes the flyer smoother, so there is less drag. Then less thrust is needed, so the plane uses less fuel and crows get less tired.
items.why: Drag works against the forward push. Anything sticking out into the moving air adds drag, so smooth shapes fly more easily.

items.p: Design one change to a paper spinner that you think will make it fall even more slowly. Say why you think so, and how you would test it fairly.
items.a: A strong answer names one change, for example wider wings, or thinner paper. It gives a reason: more wing pushes on more air as it spins. It plans a fair test: drop the old and new spinner from the same height, 3 times each, in the same still room, and compare the middle times.
items.why: A good design idea comes with a reason and a fair test. Change only one thing, so you know what made the difference.
items.context: In the Seed Spinners experiment, you make paper spinners like winged seeds. You drop them from 2 metres and time how long each takes to fall.

items.p: A girl watches the sky over Chennai at 7 in the morning and again at 1 in the afternoon on a hot, sunny day. When will she see more cheels soaring without flapping? Explain why.
items.a: At 1 in the afternoon. By then the Sun has heated the roofs and roads, and warm air rises from them in bubbles called thermals. The cheels circle inside the rising air and are carried up. Early in the morning the ground is still cool, so there are few thermals.
items.why: Soaring birds need rising warm air. Thermals are strongest when the ground is hottest.

items.p: A plane parked on the runway has big wings, but it makes no lift. Why does a plane have to move fast before it can take off?
items.a: A strong answer says that lift comes from the wings pushing air down. A parked plane's wings meet no moving air, so they push none down. Speeding along the runway sends air past the wings, until the push upwards is as big as the plane's weight.
items.why: A wing makes lift only when air moves past it. The faster the air moves, the more air it can push down.

items.p: Lakshmi and her brother Arjun argue about whether a heavier paper plane flies further.

views.says: Heavier is better. A stone thrown hard goes further than a feather, so a heavy plane will too.
Lighter is better. A light plane floats on the air, so it stays up longer and goes further.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use the Paper Clip Pilot results as evidence. Then say what the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the results: 1 clip flew further than no clip, but 3 clips flew least far. So neither 'heavier' nor 'lighter' is always right. Arjun is right that a little extra weight helps the plane push through the air. Lakshmi is right that too much weight makes it come down sooner. Where the weight goes matters too.
items.why: Both have part of the truth. A small weight on the nose balances the plane, so it glides. Too much weight makes it dive. Real plane designers weigh up the same thing.
items.context: In the Paper Clip Pilot experiment, you throw one paper plane with 0, 1 and 3 clips on its nose. You measure how far it flies.

items.p: Deep down, what is air pressure?
opts: Countless tiny air molecules bumping into a surface
items.why: Air molecules zoom about at roughly 500 metres a second and bump into everything. Those bumps are air pressure. Picking 'the wind' is close, but there is air pressure even in perfectly still air.

items.p: Under a moving wing, molecules bump a little harder than on top. What does this make?
items.why: More push underneath than on top gives an upward push: lift. Picking 'weight' mixes up gravity, which pulls down, with the air's push, which pushes up.

items.p: Scientists all agree on exactly how to explain lift in simple words.
items.why: False. They agree on what lift does, and they can calculate it very well. But they still argue about the best simple explanation.

items.p: People explain how a wing makes lift in different ways.

views.who: Followers of Daniel Bernoulli, a Swiss scientist in the 1700s
views.says: Air moves faster over the top of the wing. Faster air pushes less on the wing, so the wing is pushed up from below.

views.who: Followers of Isaac Newton, an English scientist in the 1600s
views.says: The tilted wing pushes air downwards. So the air pushes the wing upwards.

views.who: Holger Babinsky, an engineer at Cambridge University
views.says: The wing curves the moving air downwards. Curving the air makes less push above the wing and more push below it. Both rules describe the same thing.

items.ask: Which explanation would you use to explain lift to a younger child? Give your reason. Then say what one of the other explanations adds.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason, for example that Newton's is easiest to feel with a hand out of a car window. It then says what another adds, for example that Bernoulli's explains why the push on top is smaller. The best answers see that they fit together, as Babinsky says.
items.why: Each explanation is true. Scientists still argue about which is the best simple way to say it, but they agree on what lift does and can calculate it very well.

items.p: Stunt planes can fly upside down. What does this tell us?
opts: A curved top is not the only secret. The tilt of the wing matters too
The pilot holds the plane up
items.why: Upside down, the curved side is underneath. The pilot tilts the wing so it still turns air downwards. Picking 'gravity is weaker' is a natural guess. But gravity is the same whichever way up you are.

items.p: In the Hand Wing test, tilting your hand very steeply made it wobble and get pushed back. What is this called on a real wing?
items.why: When a wing is tilted too steeply, the air can't follow its top surface. It tumbles, and the wing loses most of its lift. Picking 'thrust' mixes up a backward push, drag, with a forward one.
items.context: In the Hand Wing experiment, you hold your flat hand in front of a fan and tilt it different amounts.

items.p: Mars has only about 1 hundredth as much air as Earth. What did the Ingenuity helicopter have to do to fly there?
opts: Spin its blades very fast, about 2,400 times a minute
Use the same blades and speed as a helicopter on Earth
items.why: With so little air to push, its blades had to move very fast to push enough air down. Picking 'no blades' means it is being mixed up with a rocket.
items.context: In 2021, a small NASA helicopter called Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet, Mars.

items.p: Ingenuity's blades spun about 2,400 times a minute. A ceiling fan spins about 300 times a minute. Ingenuity's blades spun ____ times as fast.
items.why: 2,400 divided by 300 is 8. You can check: 300 × 8 = 2,400.
items.context: Ingenuity was a small helicopter that flew on Mars, where the air is very thin.

items.p: People used to say 'science says bumblebees can't fly'. What is the truth?
opts: A rough sum treated the bee's wings like still plane wings. Flapping, twisting wings make much more lift
Bumblebees really can't fly. They jump
items.why: Insect wings flap and twist very fast, making whirls of air that give extra lift. A robot fly wing measured it in 1999. Picking 'lighter than air' means bees are being mixed up with balloons.

items.p: A hot-air balloon and a glider both stay in the air. How are their tricks different?
items.a: A hot-air balloon floats because the hot air inside is lighter than the cold air around it, like a cork floating in water. A glider is heavier than air. Its wings push air down, so the air pushes it up.
items.why: Balloons float. Wings lift. They are two different ways of staying up.

items.p: Many people think a bird flies by flapping their wings straight up and down. But a crow's wings push the air down AND back. Why must the air be pushed back as well as down?
items.a: A strong answer says that pushing air down gives lift, which holds the bird up. Pushing air back makes the air push the bird forward. That is thrust. Without thrust, drag would slow the bird, and the bird would have to glide down, like a flying squirrel. So a flapping bird does two jobs with one wing beat.
items.why: Every push on the air comes back as a push the other way. Air pushed down lifts the bird. Air pushed back drives the bird forward.

items.p: In the story, Farah's kite rose when she pulled the string tight. Her friend Isha says, 'If I pull harder and harder, my kite will end up straight above my head.' Is Isha right? Explain, using the words wind, string and push.
items.a: A strong answer says no. The wind pushes the kite back, away from the flyer, and the string holds it against that push. The tilted kite turns the push upwards. Straight overhead, the wind would blow flat along the kite's face instead of against it, so there would be almost no push to hold it up. So a kite always stays a little downwind of the flyer, with the string slanting.
items.why: A kite is held up by the wind pushing against a string. It needs the wind to hit its face, so it can never sit directly above the flyer.
items.context: In this unit's story, a girl called Farah can't fly her kite until she stands still and pulls the string tight. The wind pushes the kite, the string holds it, and so it rises.

items.p: A plane turns by tipping one wing down. Draw a plane from the front, tipped to its right. Draw the lift arrow at right angles to the wings. Which way will the plane turn?
items.a: A strong drawing shows the wings sloping down to the right, with the lift arrow leaning to the right too. The plane turns right, because part of the lift now pulls it sideways. A cheel turning in a thermal tips their wings in just the same way.
items.why: Lift always pushes at right angles to the wings. Tip the wings, and the lift tips too, so it pulls the flyer round in a curve.

items.p: Saturn's moon Titan has air about four times as thick as Earth's. Scientists are sending a flying drone there, called Dragonfly. Predict: will its blades need to spin faster or slower than a drone's on Earth? Explain.
items.a: Slower. Thick air gives the blades much more to push on, so each turn pushes more air down. On Mars, where the air is very thin, Ingenuity had to spin its blades very fast. Titan is the opposite.
items.why: The thicker the air, the easier it is to make lift. Thin air needs fast blades, and thick air needs only slow ones.
items.context: On Mars, where the air is very thin, the Ingenuity helicopter had to spin its blades about 2,400 times a minute.

items.p: Invent a new seed that flies. Draw it. Label the part that pushes on the air, and where the heavy seed sits. Say how the shape of your seed slows the fall.
items.a: A strong design has a wide wing, a parachute or fluff that pushes on lots of air, with the heavy seed low down or at one end, so the seed falls steadily instead of tumbling. It says how the shape slows the fall, so the wind can carry the seed far.
items.why: Real flying seeds all slow their fall by pushing on air, and they keep their heavy part in one place so they stay steady.

items.p: These flyers all stay up by pushing air down. Match each flyer to the part that does the pushing.
pairs: a tilted face held by a string
tilted wings pulled forward by engines
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: They look very different, but each one turns moving air downwards. The air pushes back up, and that push is lift.

opts: A real material made of tiny moving particles
quiz.why: Air is a real material. It fills space and pushes. Picking 'nothing' is very common, because we can't see it. An upside-down glass under water shows it is there.

quiz.p: You push an 'empty' plastic bottle, mouth down, into a bucket of water. What happens?
opts: Water can't fill it, because air inside is in the way
quiz.why: The bottle is full of air, and air takes up space. Tip the bottle a little, and bubbles of air escape while water comes in. Picking 'water rushes in' means the air isn't being counted.

quiz.p: Which force pulls a flying thing down towards the Earth?
quiz.why: Weight is gravity pulling down. Picking lift mixes up the up push and the down pull.

quiz.p: Which force pushes back against a plane moving through the air?
quiz.why: Drag is the air pushing back. Picking weight usually means every force is thought to point down.

quiz.p: How does a wing make lift?
opts: It pushes air downwards, so the air pushes it up
It pulls itself up with gravity
quiz.why: The wing turns air down, and the air pushes back up. Picking 'lighter than air' mixes wings up with balloons.

quiz.p: A kite flies best when the flyer…
opts: Stands with the wind on her back and keeps the string tight
quiz.why: The wind pushes the kite, and the tight string holds it, so the tilted kite turns that push upwards. Picking 'runs with the wind' sounds right, but then the air hardly moves past the kite.

quiz.p: In the Paper Clip Pilot test, what should change between throws?
quiz.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing. Picking 'the clips and the thrower' means testing two things at once. Then you can't tell which one made the difference.
quiz.context: In the Paper Clip Pilot experiment, you throw one paper plane with 0, 1 and 3 clips on its nose. You measure how far it flies.

quiz.p: In the Seed Spinners test, why do you drop each spinner three times?
opts: One drop can be a fluke, so three drops show the real result
Because the first drop never counts
quiz.why: A puff of air or a wobbly hand can spoil one drop. Three drops let you take the middle time. Picking 'the first never counts' is not a rule. Every careful drop counts.
quiz.context: In the Seed Spinners experiment, you make paper spinners like winged seeds. You drop them from 2 metres and time how long each takes to fall.

quiz.p: Which of these flies by flapping?
opts: A crow taking off from a wall
quiz.why: The crow beats their wings to push air down and back. A paper plane glides, and a mahogany seed spins down. Picking the seed mixes up spinning with flapping.

quiz.p: Which seed spins like a helicopter while falling?
quiz.why: Mahogany seeds have one papery wing and spin down. Picking coconut is a good thought about travelling seeds. But coconuts travel by floating on the sea, not by flying.

quiz.p: What do gliders, flying squirrels and paper planes all have in common?
opts: They have no thrust of their own, so they slowly sink as they fly
quiz.why: Gliders make lift but have no forward push, so they slowly sink. Picking 'they all flap' misses that gliding means holding still wings.

quiz.p: A sparrow and a vulture both fly by flapping. Which one beats their wings faster?
opts: The sparrow, because small wings push less air with each beat
The vulture, because a big bird needs more beats
Both beat at the same speed
quiz.why: Each beat of a small wing pushes only a little air down. So a sparrow must beat many times a second to stay up. A vulture's huge wings push lots of air with each slow beat, and they often soar without flapping at all. Picking 'the vulture' makes sense, since big birds are heavier. But their big wings push more air.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists agree about?
opts: A wing makes lift by turning moving air downwards
The one best simple way to explain lift
Exactly how the first birds began to flap
quiz.why: Scientists agree on what lift does, and can calculate it very well. They still argue about the best simple explanation, and about how bird flight began.

quiz.p: A wind tunnel film shows smoke over the top of a wing reaching the back first, long before the smoke underneath. What does this show?
opts: The 'equal time' explanation in many old books is wrong
quiz.why: The old explanation says the two streams must meet at the back. The smoke shows they don't. Picking 'wings don't need air' goes the wrong way. The film shows the wing is working on the air.

quiz.p: How did birds first begin to fly?
opts: Scientists still argue: perhaps gliding down from trees, perhaps flapping while running up slopes
Birds were always able to fly
quiz.why: Scientists agree that birds came from small feathered dinosaurs. How flapping began is still argued about. Picking 'jumped off cliffs' is a fun picture, but no evidence shows it.

quiz.p: Who was the first Indian woman to fly a plane, in 1936?
quiz.why: Sarla Thakral got her pilot's licence at 21 and flew a small plane in Lahore. Picking Kalpana Chawla is a good guess. She was an Indian-born astronaut, who flew in space much later, in 1997. Bessie Coleman was an American pilot.

applications: Planes, gliders and helicopters carry people, post and medicines across India every day.
Wind turbines have long blades shaped like wings. The wind lifts the blades around, and they make electricity.
Ceiling fans and table fans have tilted blades that push air, just like wings.
Racing cars have upside-down wings, which push them down onto the road so they grip better on corners.
Drones deliver medicines and survey farms and forests.
Kites lift cameras, weather instruments and even sails that pull big ships.
Parachutes and paragliders let people float down safely or glide for hours.
Engineers copy birds. The upturned tips on many airliner wings do a job a little like the spread feathers at a vulture's wingtips.
Seed-shaped drones and sensors, copied from mahogany and dandelion seeds, are being tested to drift over forests and fields.
Cricket and badminton: the shuttlecock's feathers add drag and keep its nose pointing forwards, like a kite's tail.
Weather scientists study thermals, because the same rising air that birds use also builds clouds and storms.
Ingenuity on Mars showed that helicopters could one day explore other planets.

open_questions.q: What is the best simple explanation of lift?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can calculate lift very well. But they still argue about how to explain it in plain words, without missing part of the story.

open_questions.q: How did birds first start to fly?
open_questions.why_open: Fossils of the first flyers are rare. Some scientists think they glided down from trees. Others think they flapped while running and climbing.

open_questions.q: How do birds find thermals they can't see?
open_questions.why_open: They may watch other birds, feel the air, or notice the ground below. Scientists are still finding out.

open_questions.q: How do migrating birds find their way across thousands of kilometres?
open_questions.why_open: They seem to use the Sun, the stars, smells and the Earth's magnetism. Exactly how they sense the magnetism is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How do swifts sleep while they fly for months without landing?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists think they may nap for moments while gliding high up. Nobody has measured it in swifts yet.

open_questions.q: Could people ever fly with strapped-on wings on Saturn's moon Titan?
open_questions.why_open: Titan has thick air and weak gravity, so scientists think it might be possible. Nobody has been there to try.

open_questions.q: Why do insects have so many different ways of flapping?
open_questions.why_open: Each kind of insect twists and beats their wings a little differently. Scientists have measured only a few of them closely.

maths.problem: In the Paper Clip Pilot test, the plane with 1 clip flew 6 metres. The plane with no clip flew 4 metres. How much further did the 1-clip plane fly?
maths.explain: To find how much further, take the smaller distance away from the bigger one. 6 take away 4 is 2. So the 1-clip plane flew 2 metres further. You can check: 4 + 2 = 6.
maths.why_maths: Taking one distance away from another tells you exactly how much a change to the plane helped.

maths.problem: In the made-up Seed Spinners results, wings 4 cm long took 1.2 seconds to fall, 7 cm wings took 1.7 seconds, and 10 cm wings took 2.2 seconds. Look for the pattern. If you made a spinner with 13 cm wings, about how long would you expect it to take?
maths.answer: About 2.7 seconds, if the pattern keeps going.
maths.explain: Each time the wings got 3 cm longer, the fall took half a second longer: 1.2, then 1.7, then 2.2. 13 cm is 3 cm longer than 10 cm, so add another half second. 2.2 + 0.5 = 2.7. A pattern is a good guess, not a promise. Build the 13 cm spinner and test it to find out.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a pattern in your results lets you predict a test you haven't done yet, and then check it.

maths.problem: In the Bird Watch, you counted a crow's wingbeats. The crow flapped 3 times every second. If the crow kept flapping at that speed, how many times would it flap in 10 seconds?
maths.explain: Each second has 3 flaps. 10 seconds is 10 lots of 3. 3 × 10 = 30. So the crow would flap 30 times. You can check by skip counting in threes: 3, 6, 9, and on to 30.
maths.why_maths: Counting for a short time and multiplying lets you work out how hard a bird works without counting every single flap.

maths.problem: In the Paper Clip Pilot test, four throws went 4 metres, 6 metres, 3 metres and 5 metres. Draw a bar chart of the throws. Which throw went furthest, and which was shortest?
maths.answer: The 6-metre throw went furthest, and the 3-metre throw was shortest. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each throw, as tall as its distance. Then look for the tallest and the shortest bar. The tallest bar is 6 metres. The shortest is 3 metres. The difference between them is 6 take away 3, which is 3 metres.
maths.why_maths: After a test you have a list of numbers. A bar chart shows the best and the worst at a glance.

roots.context: We have been learning how kites, birds and seeds fly by pushing air down. Now we ask what flying tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In your spinner test, the same paper clip fell more slowly under longer wings. A spinner speeds up until its wings push enough air down to hold its weight. Longer wings sweep through more air, so they make that push while falling more slowly. So even a very heavy plane can stay up, if its wings push enough air down.
deep_truth.habit: We think that only light things can fly, and heavy things must fall. In the 1890s, many people said a machine heavier than air could never fly. What holds a flyer up is how much air its wings push down each second.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Seed Spinners test, spinners carrying the same clip fell more slowly when their wings were longer. A jumbo jet weighs about 400 tonnes, and its wings are about 64 metres from tip to tip.

three.who_am_i: Every breath you take is the same air that holds up birds.
three.what_is_life: Birds, bats, insects and seeds each found their own way to push on the air.
three.what_is_this_world: The sky is full of air, a real material that pushes back when a wing pushes on it.

roots.thread: The same air fills your lungs, turns the ceiling fan, holds up a cheel and carries an aak seed. A wing and the air are always pushing on each other. The wing pushes the air down, and the air pushes the wing up. One push never happens without the other. So a bird stays up only together with the air around them, and the air is changed by every bird that passes.

science.text: Everything that flies with wings stays up by pushing air downwards. The air then pushes them up. This upward push is called lift.
The best simple way to explain why air speeds up over a wing is still argued about. The famous 'equal time' explanation is wrong.

other_view.view: The air holds up a bird the way a floor holds up a chair. It is a force between molecules, and saying the bird and the air fly together adds nothing that the physics does not already say.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1900 and 1901, Wilbur and Orville Wright, two bicycle makers from Ohio in the USA, tested gliders on the windy sand hills of Kitty Hawk. They had worked out how big to make the wings using tables of numbers that other inventors, such as Otto Lilienthal, had used for years. Everyone thought those numbers were right. But their 1901 glider lifted only about a third as much as the tables promised. On the way home, Wilbur said that people would not fly for a thousand years. Instead of giving up, the brothers built a wind tunnel in their bicycle shop. It was a wooden box about 2 metres long, with a fan blowing air through it. Inside, they tested more than 200 small metal wings and measured the push of the air on each one. They found that one number everyone used in these sums, worked out by John Smeaton in the 1750s, was too big. Using their own measurements, they built a new glider in 1902, and it flew well. In 1903 they added an engine and made the first powered flights.
how_we_found_out.who: Wilbur and Orville Wright, with earlier numbers from John Smeaton and Otto Lilienthal
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The numbers inventors had used for many years to work out how much a wing lifts were correct. The Wrights' wind tunnel showed that one key number was too big.
